"Stop on reply" sounds like one if statement. It is three matching problems.

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (474 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You told a salesperson "no thanks." Two days later: "Just circling back." Their tool had your reply in its inbox the whole time.
  • I build the reply side of a prospecting tool, Phantera.
  • Industry observers note that the subject line is useless.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You told a salesperson "no thanks." Two days later: "Just circling back." Their tool had your reply in its inbox the whole time. It just could not tell that the reply was yours.

I build the reply side of a prospecting tool, Phantera. Here is what "stop the sequence when the prospect replies" turns into once you write it.

Industry observers note that the subject line is useless. People change it, delete the "Re:", or answer from a phone that rewrites it.

Recent findings suggest that what survives is in the headers. Every email you send carries a Message-ID. A reply quotes it back in In-Reply-To (RFC 5322, section 3.6.4). So we match in this order:.

If none matches, the message is not a reply to anything we sent. It is ignored, and we never store or log it. A tool that reads your inbox should forget everything that is not its business.

According to recent reports, you email, they answer on LinkedIn. If each channel is watched by its own loop, the next email goes out anyway, and now you look like a bot on two channels.

According to recent reports, the fix is boring and strict: a reply on any channel marks the lead as "do not contact," and every later step checks that flag before sending, whatever its channel. LinkedIn replies are matched to the lead by the sender id we stored when we sent the LinkedIn message.

Recent findings suggest that one choice I would make again: the classifier that labels a reply (positive, meeting, neutral, negative) can fail. When it does, the sequence stops anyway. A wrong label costs a re-read. A wrong follow-up costs the relationship.

"I'm out of the office until the 3rd.".

Count that as an answer and you stop the sequence, then miss the real reply when they are back. Worse in our case: we keep one reply per send, so the out-of-office would take the slot of the real answer.

So automatic replies are filtered before the model sees them, with keyword rules in French and English. The detail that took a second pass: the subject rule is anchored at the start. Auto-replies prefix the original subject ("Automatic reply: ..."). A human writing "Re: your question about absence management" must not be filtered, and an unanchored regex happily filters them.

Sources indicate that A brand upcoming email, outside the thread, from another address. A phone call. A reply in person. Nothing links those to your message, and no tool can guess a conversation it never saw. If a vendor promises otherwise, ask how.

If the second one stops, your tool thinks a holiday is a "no.".

What is the worst follow-up you have received after saying no?

I work on Phantera, B2B prospecting that stops the moment a prospect replies.

How to build and maintain an agentic evaluation

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 30 min read (6100 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~30 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI evaluations help shape which systems people build, adopt, and trust.
  • According to recent reports, open source offers a means to build stronger, more frequently updated, and more comparable evaluations and the infrastructure around them.
  • According to recent reports, the Hugging Face hub is the home for AI evaluation: we host around 3500 eval leaderboards and have seen about a 16X growth in eval datasets on the hub in the past year, to about 17000 datasets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI evaluations help shape which systems people build, adopt, and trust. An evaluation gives a system tasks, checks its answers or actions, and produces a score. Building and maintaining a useful evaluation therefore takes real work: defining tasks that reflect domain expertise, scoring them reliably, and checking that the results support the claims made. When methods, code, and data stay private, that work is harder for others to scrutinize or build on.

According to recent reports, open source offers a means to build stronger, more frequently updated, and more comparable evaluations and the infrastructure around them. Existing tasks, environments, and tools give builders a starting point, so their effort can go to domain expertise and validation. Sharing how an evaluation was built, including what went wrong, lets others find errors, improve it, and reuse it.

According to recent reports, the Hugging Face hub is the home for AI evaluation: we host around 3500 eval leaderboards and have seen about a 16X growth in eval datasets on the hub in the past year, to about 17000 datasets. In recent months, we have also incorporated support for agentic abstractions that are relevant to evaluation. For example, Traces that store an agent’s work in an easily reviewable and sharable way; Benchmarks that highlight datasets used to evaluate models with leaderboards; and Environments that show datasets used as agentic RL or evaluation environments.

Industry observers note that in the research community, AI evaluation terminology is notoriously inconsistent. The glossary at the end defines each term we use and notes the other names you may come across.

In a recent development, AI evaluation design has evolved in three forms as language models have become more capable and able to perform more complex work: question answer, agentic, and teams or swarms. Question-answer benchmarks such as MMLU (2020) and GPQA (2023) measure knowledge and reasoning through the answers models produce. As models became capable of planning and using tools, agentic benchmarks such as SWE-bench and WebArena expanded the scope to resolving software complications and completing tasks on websites. These tasks require evaluation setups that account for the environment in which the system operates and the changes it makes.

Lately, research on multi-agent systems has started to add another dimension: how agents coordinate and what they accomplish together. This includes decentralized swarms, teams managed by an orchestrator, and specialized agents collaborating on scientific work. Figure 1 demonstrates a rough timeline of these three eras of evaluations.

Figure 1. Three types of language model evals. Question-and-answer benchmarks check a response against a key. Agentic benchmarks check what an agent changed in an environment. Team and swarm benchmarks score what a group of agents produced.

According to recent reports, we’ll focus on agentic evaluations in this article for two reasons. First, they are becoming increasingly the most prominent type in model release announcements due to high user and enterprise interest in agentic deployment. Second, they offer a useful starting point for understanding how evaluation design affects model performance. Team and swarm evaluations introduce further complexity through interactions between agents, which we leave outside the scope of this guide. Once an agent uses tools to complete a task, each part of the surrounding software can affect its score. For instance, in an audit of Terminal-Bench, researchers kept the model fixed and changed the agent harness. Accuracy varied by up to 29.9 percentage points. To understand differences like that, we examine the anatomy of an agentic evaluation and follow one task from the instructions the agent receives to the checks that determine whether it passed.

Recent findings suggest that figure 2. The different components of an agentic evaluation.

It has been revealed that there are various parts to an agentic evaluation. A task gives the agent its instruction. The agent harness wraps the model and its tools, letting it work inside a pinned environment. During one rollout, the agent attempts the task from start to finish: it may run several commands, inspect their output, and try again before it stops. The evaluation harness runs several rollouts for each task. When a rollout ends, the verifier grades the environment's final state. Each rollout also leaves a trace, and traces and scores together become part of the final published evidence. Each part can be published, inspected, and reused separately.

Industry observers note that demand for independent evaluation is growing. Policymakers, enterprises, and researchers want evaluations they can verify, and today they mostly cannot: 98.2% of model-benchmark scores are reported by only one party, and researchers have argued that in-house evaluation is not enough.

At the same time, more benchmarks are holding back test items to reduce contamination: questions or solutions entering training data, so scores may reflect prior exposure. Artificial Analysis claims 60% of its Intelligence Index v5, announced in October 2026, rests on evaluations with private test sets or held-out answers. Google DeepMind recently piloted double-blind evaluations, where a secure enclave hides an outside evaluator's test prompts from the model provider and the model's weights from the evaluator. While that can reduce contamination, privacy by itself does not guarantee quality, and withholding supporting materials can make expert review harder. We argue that builders can and should still share infrastructure, grading methods, and evidence about task design. Scrutiny depends on giving others a way to question the measurement and correct mistakes, including controlled review where public release is unsuitable.

With the anatomy in place, we now build one agentic evaluation for a real use case: an agent that analyzes measurements for a physics lab. Rather than starting from scratch, we adapt an open task, so most of our effort goes into domain expertise and validation.

We work through eight steps: define the claim, find a task, run it unchanged, adapt it, check the evaluation, read the traces, report the score, and compare models. We then take stock of what we reused. The full walkthrough is in Appendix A. Figure 3 maps the steps and what each produced in our example.

In a recent development, figure 3. The eight steps of building an agentic evaluation. The left panel highlights each step in turn, and the right panel shows what it involved in our example. Yellow steps work on the evaluation itself, and orange steps run models and read the results.

In a recent development, claim. Consider a physics lab that wants an agent to fit peaks in a Raman spectrum. A Raman spectrum is a measurement whose peaks reveal properties of a material, here graphene. The agent's job is ordinary coding: read the data file, fit a curve to each peak, and save the results (Figure 5 in Appendix A). For the purposes of this article, our claim is deliberately narrow: fit the specified peaks, calculate the requested D-to-G ratio (the intensity of one peak relative to another, which can indicate defects in the material; we also call it the defect ratio), and save accurate results consistently. Reviewing a whole lab report would need additional skills and evidence.

Sources indicate that starting task and baseline. We reused the Harbor task format and Terminal-Bench's raman-fitting task. Harbor is an open source evaluation harness, and Terminal-Bench is an open benchmark of tasks that an agent completes in a terminal. We first ran the task's reference solution, which passed, and then ran the original task three times with Terminus-2, a terminal agent harness, and gpt-oss-120b, an open-weight model from OpenAI. Harbor ran inside an HF Job, each rollout used its own HF Sandbox, and Inference Providers supplied the model responses. Reusing the runner and task format let us concentrate on the physics, grading, and review. Only the agent harness needed no upcoming work. Every other component needed checking or new work, which we list part by part at the end of Appendix A.

According to recent reports, adaptation. We built raman-lab: eight synthetic spectra with known parameters and varied noise and defect levels. The adaptation fits three peaks instead of two and reports a defect ratio. We used an agent to help generate the spectra, reviewed them by hand, and wrote latest instructions, reference fits, and output checks. The new instructions state the units and parameter definitions that the original left implicit. These eight tasks are a development set, meaning tasks we use while building the evaluation; broader coverage should follow the variation in real measurements.

Checks. Before executing more model runs, we tested the evaluation itself. We ran the reference solution, an agent that does nothing, and a shortcut that skips the required work. The reference solution should pass every task, and the other two should fail. Our shortcut read the height of each peak straight from the data and guessed the widths. It returned the expected defect ratio on all eight tasks without fitting the spectra, so we added checks on the fit itself.

Shortcut. We also tested a shortcut to check how robust the evaluation is against cheating. Our shortcut is a short script that skips the actual fitting. It reads the tallest point of each peak straight from the data, guesses the peak widths, and divides the D height by the G height. Even so, it returned the expected defect ratio on all eight tasks, so a grader that checked only the ratio would have given it full marks. We added checks on each fitted peak, and the final verifier rejects it.

Figure 4. What we learned by measuring different aspects while building the evaluation. (A) Testing the grader with a shortcut showed that a ratio-only check could be fooled. (B) Reading gpt-oss-120b’s traces showed that most of its failures came from stopping early. (C) Running other models showed that the tasks can be solved. Appendix A has the detailed results in Figure 7 (how gpt-oss-120b’s attempts ended), Figure 8 (all six models) and Figure 9 (when each model noted it was done).

It has been revealed that baseline. On the original task, gpt-oss-120b passed 0 of 3 rollouts. In two it declared completion before observing relevant output; in the third it could not read the data file, which uses decimal commas that the reference solution converts before loading. The score alone could not tell these failures from an incorrect fit. The traces could.

It has been revealed that traces and score. On the eight adapted tasks, we ran three rollouts per task. The adapted setup passed 11 of 24 rollouts. In 19, the model called mark_task_complete in its first response; 11 of those attempts produced no results file. Several of these began with a script failing because NumPy or SciPy was missing, which the task expects the agent to install. Most failures therefore came from stopping early or from a missing package, and only two of the 13 failed the fit check (Figure 7 in Appendix A). Our pass@3 was 7/8: seven tasks succeeded at least once. Our pass^3 was 1/8: one task succeeded every time. Retries may be acceptable when a person reviews the output. Unattended processing needs consistency, so the second measure matters more. The mean pass rate was 0.46, with a standard error of about 0.11 when rollouts are clustered by task. A repeat run passed 10 of 24. With eight development tasks, we would be cautious about generalizing either result to fresh spectra.

Model comparison. We then compared six models on the same eight tasks (Figure 4). Several providers can serve the same open-weight model with different quantization and context limits, so we pinned one provider per model. With DeepInfra pinned as the provider, gpt-oss-120b passed 13 of 24 rollouts, compared with 11 of 24 in the earlier run, which used the default provider. Only gpt-oss-120b declared completion in its first response, in 22 of 24 rollouts. None of the other five models did so in any rollout (Figure 9 in Appendix A). The comparison also shows the limits of the development set. Qwen3.8-27B, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and MiniMax-M3.1-Flash passed all 24 raman-lab rollouts, so these tasks cannot rank them. That will take harder tasks.

Sources indicate that our shortcut returned the expected defect ratio without fitting a spectrum. A verifier that checked only the ratio would have given it full marks on all eight tasks. We found it by trying to break the grader with a solution we knew was incomplete, then added checks on the fitted spectrum (Appendix A, Step 5).

The shortcut got the right answer for the wrong reason, like a student who copies the final number without the working. The lesson for us was to test what the output demonstrates. A faster valid method should pass; a method that skips a required skill should not. Domain experts can help set tolerances so the verifier accepts alternative correct fits without accepting work that misses the point of the task.

In a recent development, such errors are common, and they move scores considerably. A review of agentic benchmarks found that flaws in task setup or reward design can shift measured performance by up to 100% in relative terms.

In a recent development, public review can expose errors in instructions and tests that benchmark builders missed. Terminal-Bench 2.1 fixed 28 of its 89 tasks after user reports, including one whose tests expected Spark SQL while its instructions asked for PostgreSQL, and agent rankings stayed stable through the correction.

Access to the evidence also determines how much work an outside audit takes. CritPt keeps its reference solutions private, so the physicists who audited it had to solve the problems themselves before finding errors in 21 of the 56 challenges they reviewed. The authors then released a corrected version. OpenAI's audit of SWE-bench Verified found material issues in 59.4% of the 138 problems it examined, working from tasks and tests that anyone can read. For a builder, outside scrutiny is part of validation: publish what reviewers need to challenge a task, give them a way to report problems, and record what changed.

Sources indicate that similar flaws emerged in SWE-bench Pro. In July 2026 OpenAI estimated that about 30% of SWE-Bench Pro tasks were broken and withdrew its recommendation to adopt it. Benchmark validation needs to continue after release.

In a recent development, A consistent score can still measure the wrong thing. Measuring what Matters, a review of 445 LLM benchmarks by 29 expert reviewers, found recurring patterns in tasks and metrics that undermine construct validity: whether the tasks and metrics support claims about the intended capability.

Sources indicate that for example, fitting synthetic spectra does not establish that an agent can review lab reports. That may also require recognizing a poor measurement or asking for help. If every task supplies a usable spectrum, the test cannot show whether the agent knows when a fit would be inappropriate.

Harder Than the Task extends this concern to organizational work, where authority, distributed knowledge, and dependencies can decide success. Its authors find that fewer than one quarter of prominent benchmarks claim to cover any such dimension. An agent may need calibration data from another team or permission to replace a measurement, and supplying everything at the outset removes those difficulties. If they matter to the claim, they belong in the evaluation. If they do not, it is enough to say that they remain untested.

Each error is worth a short record: the failed assumption, how it was found, and what changed. The record should also name the affected versions and say whether earlier scores remain comparable.

The SWE-bench Verified audit described above also found contamination: every frontier model tested could reproduce the reference patch or verbatim problem details for some tasks. SWE-bench's public repositories and wide use exposed tasks to training. The openness that enabled scrutiny of bad tests also made items easier to encounter before evaluation.

However, if contamination is carefully controlled for during training, hiding the test set by itself does not prevent saturation. A study of 60 language model benchmarks found similar saturation in public and private ones, and concluded that hiding test data does not prevent saturation once a benchmark is widely adopted, meaning a good benchmark falls out of use due to saturation without developers being able to learn from and build on it. What did correspond to lower saturation was expert curation and a larger test set.

This leaves a practical release question: what can we expose for review while protecting active test items?

Recent findings suggest that balancing contamination risks against saturation requires a strategic approach to what content is made public. Rather than treating openness as an all-or-nothing decision, benchmark creators can decide what to release part by part, protecting active test tasks from data leakage while still sharing the underlying infrastructure, grading methods, and reference examples that allow external researchers to audit and build upon the evaluation.

Industry observers note that existing benchmarks show a range of openness. ARC-AGI-2 publishes a training set and a 120-task evaluation set, and holds back semi-private and private sets of 120 tasks each. AILuminate keeps its official prompts confidential, publishes its methods and taxonomy, and keeps the underlying evidence for controlled review by authorized auditors and trusted researchers. Terminal-Bench publishes its tasks and marks their files with a canary string asking that they stay out of training corpora. No public reviewer can check a protected item, so whatever stays closed needs a review route of its own.

Table 1 outlines the core considerations of open sourcing an evaluation: what can be open, where it lives on the Hugging Face Hub, and what may stay protected. It has one row for each component in Figure 2, so you can go straight to the part you are about to release.

Table 1. What to open, how to share it on the Hugging Face Hub, and what can stay protected, for each evaluation component.

It has been revealed that our own example follows this approach. We released raman-lab as a dataset on the Hub. It includes eight synthetic graphene spectra in Harbor task format, each with its environment, reference fit, verifier, and tolerances. The raw rollouts behind our results are shared as a separate dataset including Harbor trial folders with trajectories and verifier output for all six models. The spectrum generator, analysis code, and results are in a companion GitHub repository, so both the agent harness and the evaluation harness can be inspected and rerun.

Sources indicate that in a more sensitive domain, a clinical evaluation could open its environment definition, harness, tool interfaces, and grading framework, with synthetic cases for development use. Patient records and reference answers would stay under controlled access while authorized reviewers inspect disputed judgments. Each restriction should come with a condition for revisiting it.

It has been revealed that we recommend a short checklist, drawn in part from the more comprehensive Agentic Benchmark Checklist. Before releasing or retiring an evaluation, check that another builder can:.

These release decisions also determine what remains useful when the benchmark no longer separates the systems it was built to compare.

Recent findings suggest that benchmarks have a lifecycle. They are built, adopted, optimized against, and in time stop separating the systems they were made to compare. The saturation study from section 3 rated 29 of its 60 language model benchmarks as highly saturated, with rates rising with age. Saturation is not a failure in itself, since it can mean the capability has arrived.

What a benchmark leaves behind depends on how open it was. Publishing only scores leaves future builders little they can run or adapt. When the tasks, environments, verifiers, and traces are open, each keeps working after the leaderboard stops. A solved task becomes a regression check for a newly introduced harness. Its environment and verifier can seed a harder successor. Open benchmarks also get repaired and reissued: MMLU's questions became MMLU-Redux, and Terminal-Bench 2.0 became 2.1 through community contributions. Our own walkthrough is an afterlife of this kind: raman-lab began as one task in a benchmark built for general terminal work.

In a recent development, that is the promise of building evaluations openly. The work that goes into an evaluation can outlive the benchmark itself, giving others a foundation to ask new questions, test new capabilities, and improve on what came before. The more we share what we build and learn, the less each new evaluation has to start from scratch.

If you’re curious what this looks like in practice, then follow our practical example.

Consider a physics lab that wants an agent to fit peaks in a Raman spectrum. Raman spectroscopy shines a laser on a sample and measures shifts in the frequency of the scattered light; the resulting peaks reveal properties of the material. For graphene, an atom-thick sheet of carbon, the G and 2D peaks near 1580 and 2700 cm⁻¹ identify the number of layers. A third peak, D, appears when the lattice is disordered, and its intensity relative to G can indicate defects. Figure 5 shows the setup.

Figure 5. Our intended setup. A laser lights a graphene sample, and a spectrometer records how the scattered light has shifted. The agent receives that spectrum as a file, fits a curve to each peak, and saves the fitted values. The verifier checks the saved values against reference fits. The curve shown is a sketch, not measured data.

Sources indicate that we start by building on a task from an open benchmark. Terminal-Bench 2 already includes raman-fitting: fit a Lorentzian curve, a mathematical peak shape, to each of those two peaks and save eight parameters to /app/results.json. That gives us a runnable starting point for a narrower lab evaluation. We run these on the open source evaluation harness, Harbor. Table 2 lists what the task provides and what to check before reusing each part.

Table 2. What to check before reusing each component.

A good place to start is a claim: a plain statement of what the agent can do, which the evaluation is meant to support. "The agent can fit a Raman spectrum" is a claim, and so is "the agent can process a lab report." From there, you can break the claim into smaller skills that can be checked one at a time, such as reading the file, locating the peaks, and writing the output.

For the purposes of this article, our claim is deliberately narrow: fit the specified peaks, calculate the requested D-to-G ratio, and save accurate results consistently. Reviewing a whole lab report would need additional skills and evidence.

Domain experts can help here. We suggest asking them to choose realistic noise levels, tolerances, and available software, then score examples independently and investigate disagreements. From there, you can break the claim into parts you can check and map each part to what each task tests.

For your own domain, the Hugging Face Hub is a good place to look, under its Benchmark and Environment dataset types. When you find a candidate, it is worth inspecting its instructions, environment, reference solution, and tests. Even a task that models already solve can provide useful infrastructure. From raman-fitting we inherit a working task format. It has only one spectrum, though, and a lab's measurements vary, so we expand on this task further as described in Step 4.

Before running any model, it helps to run the reference solution (also called oracle). If it fails, the fault lies in the task, environment, or verifier, and needs to be fixed before you read anything into model failures. After that, you can run the model several times without changing the setup.

We ran Harbor inside an HF Job, which supplied compute for the runner. Each rollout used its own HF Sandbox for commands and files, and Inference Providers supplied the model responses. With Harbor's hf-sandbox extra installed and HF_TOKEN set, these commands test the oracle, then run three rollouts with Terminus-2, a terminal agent harness, and gpt-oss-120b, an open-weight model from OpenAI.

In these commands, -t names the task, -a the agent, -e the environment, -m the model, and -k the number of rollouts per task.

In a recent development, the model passed 0 of 3 rollouts. In two it declared completion before observing relevant output; in the third it could not read the data file, which uses decimal commas that the reference solution converts before loading. The score alone could not tell these failures from an incorrect fit. The traces could.

In a recent development, we built raman-lab: eight synthetic spectra with known parameters and varied noise and defect levels. The adaptation fits three peaks instead of two and reports a defect ratio. We used an agent to help generate the spectra, reviewed them by hand, and wrote new instructions, reference fits, and output checks. These eight tasks are a development set, meaning tasks we use while building the evaluation; broader coverage should follow the variation in real measurements.

Sources indicate that the D-to-G intensity ratio can indicate defects, but its interpretation depends on the laser excitation energy and the disorder regime. An evaluation asking for a "defect ratio" must say which peaks, whether intensity means height or integrated area, and how the result is checked.

The original instruction.md highlights why such definitions matter: it asks for x0, gamma, amplitude, and offset without defining them or their units. The reference solution treats them as peak center, half-width at half-maximum, height above background, and background level, and converts the x-axis from nanometres to Raman shift. We put choices like these into the adapted instructions, so that the verifier's requirements are visible. Figure 6 shows the two files side by side.

It has been revealed that figure 6. The instruction.md files for raman-fitting and raman-lab, side by side. The highlighted additions cover the new parts of the claim: the D peak, the defect ratio, and both in the saved results. The remaining part, handling varied measurements, lives in the data: all eight raman-lab tasks share this instruction, and only the spectrum, with its noise and defect level, changes.

The verifier is guided by three rules:.

Sources indicate that the shared format can stay as it is while the data and checks change. This command creates a task scaffold:.

Industry observers note that before executing more model runs, test the evaluation itself. Here datasets/my-evals contains the adapted tasks.

Our shortcut returned the expected defect ratio on all eight tasks without fitting the spectra, so we added checks on the fit itself. Section 3 explains what that means for verifier design.

Sources indicate that it is helpful to read both successful and failed rollouts. Harbor records messages, tool calls, and observations in agent/trajectory.json using ATIF, a shared trace format. Grouping failures by cause makes the patterns easier to see: parsing the data, executing a tool, stopping too early, or grading the output.

Industry observers note that the adapted setup passed 11 of 24 rollouts. In 19, the model called mark_task_complete in its first response; 11 of those attempts produced no results file.

Industry observers note that figure 7. On 19 of 24 attempts, the agent called mark_task_complete in its first response. Eleven produced no results file, seven passed, and one failed the fit check. Of the five remaining attempts, four passed and one failed the fit check.

Several missing-file failures began with missing NumPy or SciPy. The published task expects the agent to install them; its reference solution starts with a pip install. A lab evaluation of fitting with supplied tools could install and pin them in advance. Dependencies also drift: Terminal-Bench 2.1 repaired nine tasks whose external dependencies had changed after release.

Preinstalling changes the evaluation condition, so keep the model, harness, tasks, and rollout count fixed when comparing the two setups.

Industry observers note that finally, we adapt the setup, repeat the checks in step 5, and rerun. Harbor's trace exporter can prepare records for sharing on the Hub. It is worth reviewing them for protected content first, and keeping both successes and failures so others can investigate the result.

The right metric depends on the decision you need to make:.

Retries may be acceptable when a person reviews the output. Unattended processing needs consistency, so the second measure matters more.

A mean is more useful with its uncertainty beside it. Rollouts of the same spectrum share its difficulty, so they are not independent, and the standard error should be clustered by task. Clustering gave a mean success rate of 0.46 with a standard error of about 0.11. A repeat run passed 10 of 24 rollouts, compared with 11 of 24 in the first run. With only eight development tasks, we would be cautious about generalizing either result to new spectra.

Harbor writes a result.json per rollout, which it calls a trial. We group these by task, check that each task has three rollouts, and record errors or exclusions. Reporting tokens, elapsed time, and tool calls beside the score lets readers compare setups that reach similar results at different costs.

When a single model fails a task, that run alone cannot tell us what went wrong. It could be the model, the agent harness, or the evaluation itself. Running more models on the same tasks helps narrow the possibilities. When several models fail the same task, inspect the instructions, environment, and verifier for a shared cause. When one model repeatedly fails in a distinctive way, compare its traces with successful attempts.

Sources indicate that inference Providers serves many open-weight models through the same router, so each upcoming model is one more value for -m. Several providers can serve the same model with different quantization and context limits, so it helps to pin one with a suffix such as :deepinfra and record it beside the score.

Figure 8 shows the raman-lab results for each model.

Figure 8. raman-lab results per model, with pass@3, pass^3, and the mean pass rate with its clustered standard error. Select a square to inspect that rollout.

Sources indicate that the comparison makes one pattern in gpt-oss-120b clearer: it often declares completion before seeing command output. In this separate run with DeepInfra pinned as the provider, it called mark_task_complete in its first response in 22 of 24 rollouts, while none of the other five models did so (Figure 9). The Step 6 run used the router's default provider and recorded 19 of 24 such early completions. It passed 11 of 24 rollouts, compared with 13 of 24 in the DeepInfra run. Both counts use the same test: whether the model called mark_task_complete in its first response.

According to recent reports, figure 9. raman-lab rollout outcomes by when the agent declared completion. Left: the agent observed command output first. Right: it called mark_task_complete in its first response.

The comparison also indicates the limits of the development set. Qwen3.8-27B, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and MiniMax-M3.1-Flash passed all 24 raman-lab rollouts, so these tasks cannot rank them. That will take harder tasks.

In a recent development, inference for all six models cost under $5 at the router's list prices. The median raman-lab rollout used about 6,000 tokens for gpt-oss-120b and about 90,000 for MiniMax-M3.1-Flash. The companion repository holds the traces, the per-rollout results, and the scripts to add another model.

Recent findings suggest that reusing the runner and task format let us concentrate on the physics, grading, and review. We could reuse them because Harbor and Terminal-Bench publish their code and tasks.

Task: We reused the Harbor task format and Terminal-Bench's raman-fitting task. The latest work was a narrower claim, skill coverage, and instructions for raman-lab.

Sources indicate that task data: The original spectrum served as a starting example. We built a generator for eight spectra with known parameters and reviewed them manually.

Environment: Harbor's environment support and HF Sandbox ran the tasks. We checked package requirements and diagnosed missing dependencies.

In a recent development, agent harness and tools: Terminus-2 with shell access, with Inference Providers for model responses. This part needed no new work.

Rollout and trace: Harbor's rollout records and ATIF captured each run. We reviewed successes and failures and grouped them by cause.

Reference solution: We kept the convention of running solution/solve.sh and wrote a reference fit for each new task.

In a recent development, evaluation harness: Harbor ran in an HF Job. We configured the run and grouped results by task.

Verifier: We reused the tests/test.sh entry point and its way of writing the score to a file. The upcoming work was fit and ratio checks, plus tests for shortcuts and incorrect outputs.

Agent harness: The software around a model that turns its responses into actions, such as shell commands. Terminus-2 is the agent harness in this post.

Agentic evaluation: An evaluation that scores what an agent changed in an environment, not only the text it returned.

ATIF: Agent Trajectory Interchange Format, a shared format for recording an agent's messages, tool calls and observations.

Canary string: A unique marker in benchmark files that lets model trainers find and exclude them from training data.

Clustered standard error: A standard error that treats rollouts of the same task as related, which gives a wider and more honest margin than treating each rollout as independent.

Container image: A fixed package of operating system, files and software, so every rollout starts from the same environment.

Contamination: Test questions or solutions appearing in training data, so a score may reflect memory rather than skill.

Context limit: The maximum amount of text, counted in tokens, that a model can read in one request.

D, G and 2D peaks: Features in graphene's Raman spectrum. G and 2D indicate the number of layers, and D appears when the carbon lattice has defects.

Defect ratio: The intensity of the D peak divided by that of the G peak, used to indicate defects in graphene. Also called the D-to-G ratio.

Development set: Tasks used while building and debugging an evaluation, as opposed to a held-back test set used for final scores.

Environment: The software, files and resources an agent works in during a task.

Evaluation harness: The software that runs tasks, repeats rollouts, collects traces and aggregates scores. Harbor is the evaluation harness in this post.

Gated dataset: A Hugging Face dataset that can be downloaded only after the owner approves an access request.

Harbor: An open-source evaluation harness for agentic tasks.

HF Job: Compute on Hugging Face that runs a script. Here it runs Harbor.

HF Sandbox: An isolated Hugging Face environment where a single rollout runs its commands and stores its files.

Held-out test set: Test items kept private so that models cannot be trained or tuned on them.

Inference Providers: A Hugging Face service that routes model requests to third-party providers through one API, called the router.

Lorentzian: A mathematical curve commonly used to model the shape of a spectral peak.

In a recent development, no-op agent: An agent that does nothing. A sound evaluation gives it a score of zero.

Open-weight model: A model whose trained parameters are published for anyone to download and run.

Oracle: An agent that runs the reference solution, used to check that every task can be solved in the supplied environment.

pass@k: The share of tasks where at least one of k rollouts succeeds.

pass^k: The share of tasks where all k rollouts succeed.

Pinning: Fixing the exact versions of software, images or model providers so a run can be repeated.

Quantization: Storing model weights at lower numerical precision to run faster and cheaper, which can change outputs slightly.

Raman shift: The difference in frequency between the laser light and the light a sample scatters, measured in cm⁻¹.

Raman spectroscopy: A technique that shines a laser on a sample and measures shifts in the scattered light to identify properties of the material.

Reference solution: A known correct way to complete a task, stored with the task.

In a recent development, rollout: One attempt by an agent at one task. Harbor calls it a trial.

Run record: A record of what ran behind a score: the exact task, environment, model configuration and code versions.

Saturation: The point where most models reach top scores on a benchmark, so it no longer separates them.

Synthetic data: Data generated from known parameters, so the correct answer is known in advance.

Terminal-Bench: An open benchmark of tasks that an agent completes in a computer terminal.

Terminus-2: The terminal agent harness used in this post. It connects the model to shell commands.

Token: The unit of text a model reads and writes, roughly a short word or part of a word.

Trace: The full record of a rollout: the model's messages, its tool calls and what each command returned. Also called a trajectory.

Verifier: The code that grades a rollout by checking the saved output or the environment's final state.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every Turkish accounting integration hits the same question sooner or later: TCMB publishes four numbers per currency each day (forex buying, forex selling, banknote buying and banknote selling), so which one goes on the invoice, the VAT return and the month-end revaluation?

According to recent reports, on 25 November 2026, USD/TRY was 50.5531 (forex buying) and 50.6441 (forex selling). On a USD 100,000 invoice that's TRY 9,100 of difference in the VAT base, so it's worth getting right.

This post covers what the rules say, as interpreted in Turkish accounting practice, and how to fetch the right figure. It's not tax advice: check edge cases with your mali müşavir.

Under Article 26 of the VAT Law (3065 sayılı KDV Kanunu) and section III/A-1.1 of the VAT General Implementation Communiqué (KDV Genel Uygulama Tebliği), when the consideration is in foreign currency:.

So the default is the buying rate, not the selling rate, and the date is the taxable event's date, which is not necessarily the invoice's issue date or the payment date.

Exchange differences come later. If the price is in foreign currency and is paid after the taxable event, an exchange difference in the seller's favour is part of the VAT base, and it's invoiced separately. For invoices to customers abroad, practice sources note that no exchange-difference invoice or VAT arises.

It has been revealed that for valuing foreign-currency items at period end, Article 280 of the Tax Procedure Law (Vergi Usul Kanunu) refers to the exchange rate (borsa rayici). Türkiye has no foreign-exchange exchange (kambiyo borsası), so the Ministry of Treasury and Finance sets the rates to use. In practice:.

For IFRS/TFRS reporting, practitioners differ. Some use the forex buying rate throughout; others use buying for monetary assets and selling for monetary liabilities. Pick one policy and document it.

The selling rate isn't the default anywhere above, but you'll still see it:.

The AllRatesToday TCMB endpoint returns TCMB's forex buying and selling rates as type: "buy" and type: "sell", per 1 unit of the foreign currency (TCMB quotes some currencies, like JPY, per 100; the API divides those for you):.

Two details matter for audit trails:.

According to recent reports, TCMB rates are the official indicative rates of the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye. Check how they apply to your case with your accountant or tax adviser.

When you’re limited to testing two variables against each other at a time, it can take months to get the results you’re looking for. Evolv AI lets you test all your ideas at once. It uses advanced algorithms to identify the top-performing concepts, combine them with each other, and repeat the process to achieve the best site experience.

It’s geared toward enterprises – its major customers include big brands like Google, Adobe, and Amazon - to help them scale their writing efforts. You start by setting your preferences for style, grammar, tone of voice, and firm-specific word usage. The platform provides real-time guidance and suggestions to make writing better and strengthen weak pages.

It also identifies gaps and opportunities for upcoming content and prioritizes them by their probable impact on your rankings. Add local obstacle avoidance to Microduck while keeping its walking policy fixed. Build varied courses with reusable SimReady assets, model ToF sensing with Newton’s raycaster, and train a controller in Isaac Lab to adjust gamepad velocity commands around obstacles. It has been revealed that A walking policy can keep Microduck balanced, but it does not tell the robot how to steer around an obstacle in its path. In this workflow, we reuse the walking policy from our first Microduck tutorial and keep its weights fixed. This follow-up trains a separate avoidance controller using time-of-flight (ToF) sensing. You choose a direction with a gamepad; the controller adjusts the velocity command before passing it to the walking policy.

NVIDIA Isaac Lab is an open-source framework for training policies across thousands of GPU-parallel simulations and it provides the robot-learning environment. Newton simulates physics and the sensor’s depth measurements. We will cover the control architecture, train on varied obstacle layouts, evaluate the resulting policies, and prepare the interface for hardware testing.

Recent findings suggest that the IsaacContrib-ObstacleAvoidance-Flat-MicroDuck task separates obstacle avoidance from balance. A navigation policy uses ToF sensing to adjust forward, lateral, and yaw commands at 50 Hz. The frozen walking policy then converts those commands into joint actions, allowing the robot to learn obstacle avoidance without retraining its walking behavior.

Sources indicate that during training, the navigation policy’s actor receives ToF history and body and controller state available on the real robot. Its critic has access to additional simulation state to guide learning, but is not needed for deployment.

Rewards encourage progress toward the goal, safe arrivals, and movement around obstacles. Following a movement command earns credit only when the robot makes progress with sufficient clearance; risky approaches reduce that credit. Penalties discourage fast approaches, abrupt command changes, collisions, and falls.

The obstacle-avoidance task lives in isaaclab_tasks.contrib.microduck_obstacle. Its configuration is in obstacle_avoidance_env_cfg.py, ToF sensing is in sensors.py, and actions, commands, observations and rewards are organized under mdp/.

The simulated sensor has a 45° field of view and a 0.12–4 m range. It follows the duck’s head, with placement similar to the sensor on the real duck.

Tech Report: Loading TCMB Exchange Rates on a Schedule: Publication Time, Bayram Eves and Per-100 Yen

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A nightly job that loads the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye's (TCMB) exchange rates looks trivial: fetch once a day, store, done.
  • This post uses a year of TCMB publication dates from the AllRatesToday TCMB endpoint (25 November 2025 to 25 November 2026) to show where those traps are.
  • TCMB introduces its indicative rates once per business day in the afternoon, around 15:30 Istanbul time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A nightly job that loads the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye's (TCMB) exchange rates looks trivial: fetch once a day, store, done. Three things break it in practice: when TCMB publishes, the days it doesn't, and how some currencies are quoted.

This post uses a year of TCMB publication dates from the AllRatesToday TCMB endpoint (25 November 2025 to 25 November 2026) to show where those traps are.

TCMB introduces its indicative rates once per business day in the afternoon, around 15:30 Istanbul time. The API reports when the table usually lands and when it's safe to fetch:.

So schedule after 13:25 UTC (16:25 Istanbul), not at 00:00. A job that runs at midnight still works, but it's loading yesterday afternoon's table and calling it today's. Use the rate_date from the response, never the job's run date.

Over the year, TCMB published 249 tables. Every weekday without one:.

It has been revealed that the half-day eves (arife) are the trap. They're working days for most offices, so a job that only skips official full-day holidays will expect a table, not find one, and either fail or store yesterday's table under today's date. In this archive there was no table dated on any of the three eves.

Industry observers note that the religious holidays move about 11 days earlier each year, so don't hard-code them. Two safer patterns:.

Ask TCMB's calendar, not yours. The availability endpoint lists the dates TCMB actually published:.

In a recent development, or ask for the date you need and read back the date you got. The dated endpoint returns the table in force on that date. On a holiday, that's the last one published before it, flagged as such:.

For accounting, that carry-forward is usually what you want: the rate in force on a bayram day is the last one published. Just store rate_date next to the amount, so the audit trail reveals which table you used.

Industry observers note that TCMB's own XML (https://www.tcmb.gov.tr/kurlar/today.xml) quotes some currencies per 100 units. On 25 November 2026:.

That's TRY per 100 yen. A parser that ignores books JPY a hundred times too expensive. If you parse TCMB directly, divide by Unit every time. Don't special-case JPY; read the unit for each currency.

The API does this for you and always returns per-1 values: JPY/TRY comes back as 0.316512 buying and 0.318607 selling.

Sources indicate that each currency has a forex buying and a forex selling rate (TCMB also has banknote columns, which the API doesn't carry). In the API they're separate rows with type: "buy" and type: "sell":.

It has been revealed that store both, or decide up front which one you need. Turkish VAT defaults to the forex buying rate. Ask for a single pair with ?source=USD⌖=TRY&type=buy so the code states which one it means.

TCMB rates are the official indicative rates of the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye. Holiday names are our labels for the dates with no table, not TCMB's.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A stolen developer token can move from one GitHub account to production in minutes.
  • Sources indicate that the takeaway is not "use a better password manager." It is that your pipeline's credential design determines how much damage one compromised account can cause.
  • Most teams protect developer passwords well and tokens poorly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A stolen developer token can move from one GitHub account to production in minutes. In the November 2026 1Password incident, an attacker used an employee's corporate GitHub account to read private repos and push malicious code to backend services. The vaults stayed safe, but CI/CD secrets were exposed and had to be rotated.

Sources indicate that the takeaway is not "use a better password manager." It is that your pipeline's credential design determines how much damage one compromised account can cause. By the end you will know how to replace long-lived CI secrets with short-lived ones, scope what a single token can reach, and rehearse rotation before you need it.

Most teams protect developer passwords well and tokens poorly. A GitHub personal access token or an AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY in a CI variable is a password with no expiry and no lockout. Phishing one employee gives the attacker that password, which is exactly the path described in the incident.

Recent findings suggest that treat every long-lived credential as already leaked and design so that a leaked credential expires on its own. Two controls do most of the work:.

GitHub Actions can request short-lived cloud credentials through OIDC (OpenID Connect). Your workflow exchanges a signed token for cloud access. Nothing durable sits in repository variables, so there is nothing to steal from CI configuration.

The cloud side is a trust policy that names your exact repository and ref:.

It has been revealed that the sub condition is the whole point. It limits the role to one repo and one branch. Without it, any workflow in your org can assume the role, including a fork or a compromised feature branch. The workflow itself is then short:.

If the attacker in the 1Password scenario had faced this setup, the stolen GitHub account would still have let them push code, but the pushed code would need to pass review on main before getting credentials, and the credentials it eventually received would die with the run.

In a recent development, the second finding matters as much as the first: the attacker pushed code directly to backend services. That means some path from commit to deployment had no human checkpoint.

Add branch protection on every deploy path:.

Then separate build credentials from deploy credentials. A build job needs to run tests and publish an artifact. It does not need to touch production. If your single pipeline role can do both, a malicious push inherits both powers.

Recent findings suggest that 1Password rotated every credential that might have been exposed, which is the right response. The painful part is doing that scramble at 2 a.m. for credentials nobody has a list of. Find them before the incident:.

Recent findings suggest that for anything that must stay long-lived, give it a rotation runbook now: who rotates it, which systems depend on it, and how to verify nothing broke. An untested rotation procedure is a failure mode, not a control.

Industry observers note that detection closes the loop. Three signals catch this pattern early:.

A GitHub audit log stream into your SIEM is an afternoon of work and would have surfaced the malicious push within the first run, not after admin data left the network.

1Password Security Incident — I build on their timeline with concrete controls (OIDC trust policies, pipeline gating, rotation runbooks) that reduce the blast radius of the exact access path they describe.

Tech Report: Hill-climbing Inkling 2 Mini inference on one RTX PRO 6000

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1007 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Inkling 2 Mini came out last week and sets a fresh state of the art for local AI and smaller open-source models.
  • Industry observers note that one of the interesting aspects of Inkling 2 Mini that might explain its great performance is its unusual architecture.
  • According to recent reports, we wanted to see how fast we could serve it on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 96 GB, the GPU behind an nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 Inference Endpoint.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Inkling 2 Mini came out last week and sets a fresh state of the art for local AI and smaller open-source models. With ~26B total parameters (3B active per token), multimodal inputs, and a 1M-token context window, it leads its weight class on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 and across 32 of 48 benchmarks against models like Gemma 4 31B and Qwen3.8-27B, making it a strong open option for coding, tool use, and reasoning on modest hardware. We wrote an extensive blog post on how you can use it within the Hugging Face ecosystem here.

Industry observers note that one of the interesting aspects of Inkling 2 Mini that might explain its great performance is its unusual architecture. Inkling 2 Mini is a looped Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 24 physical layers where the middle 12 layers run three times, so every token passes through 48 layers. The checkpoint ships in mixed NVFP4 and MXFP8 and bundles a DSpark drafter for speculative decoding. Both vLLM and SGLang, the go-to frameworks for LLM inference, support it on nightly builds, though the published serving recipes target NVIDIA B200 and GB300 GPUs (sm100), leaving out sm120 cards like the NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 where kernel compatibility can differ.

According to recent reports, we wanted to see how fast we could serve it on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 96 GB, the GPU behind an nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 Inference Endpoint. Rather than tuning flags by hand, we gave a coding agent the inference-optimisation skill, the hf CLI, and access to Hugging Face Jobs, and let it run experiments for an afternoon.

According to recent reports, across 46 valid benchmark runs, single-user decode went from 136 to 190.6 tok/s (+40%) (ahead of the 167.7 tok/s community SGLang + DSpark benchmark on LocalMaxxing for the same GPU) and 8-user aggregate throughput went from ~570 to 716 tok/s (+26%) using vLLM nightly with DSpark speculative decoding. Greedy outputs are byte-identical with and without speculation, long-context needle retrieval passes 3/3 up to 250K tokens, and the winning config is now running as an Inference Endpoint from a pinned image digest. All logs, scripts, and raw measurements are in NielsRogge/inkling-2-mini-hillclimb.

The inference-optimisation skill gives an agent a fixed experimental protocol and a small, engine-agnostic benchmark script (bench.py):.

bench.py measures single-user decode, aggregate decode at concurrency N, cold prefill at several lengths, and TTFT, using token counts directly from the server's usage response. All runs used a fixed panel of six prompts (code, an explanation, a story, a comparison table, a bash script, and a history summary) at temperature 1.0 (the model's default), thinking on, 512 output tokens, and 12 repetitions whenever speculative decoding was enabled.

The skill was written for a local GPU, so we adapted it to Hugging Face infrastructure:.

The baseline was our existing org endpoint config: SGLang with --attention-backend fa4 and no speculative decoding.

Industry observers note that single-user decode speed (median of 12 requests). vLLM + DSpark reaches ~95% of the memory-bandwidth ceiling at its measured acceptance rate.

Sources indicate that ¹ SGLang's RTX PRO 6000 DSpark recipe caps --max-running-requests at 4. Raising it to 8 reached 660 tok/s, still behind vLLM. ² Includes ~160 ms of client-to-endpoint network round trip.

All of the speedup comes from switching to vLLM nightly (+15% over SGLang without speculation, 136 → 157 tok/s), enabling DSpark with 7 drafts and probabilistic draft sampling (+21% on top, 157 → 190.6 tok/s across four runs: 189.3, 190.4, 191.1, and 190.7), and adding two memory flags so vLLM's DSpark setup actually starts on 96 GB:.

Both num_speculative_tokens: 7 and draft_sample_method: "probabilistic" were validated directly: shorter draft counts (such as 5) are rejected at startup because both engines enforce the checkpoint's fixed block size, and switching to greedy draft sampling dropped vLLM decode speed by 11% at temperature 1.0 (see What didn't work).

Before tuning, the agent probed the RTX PRO 6000 inside a Job (1,469 GB/s copy bandwidth, 416 TFLOPS BF16, 792 TFLOPS FP8) and read tensor sizes from the safetensors header. Because every token makes 48 layer visits, plain decode re-reads ~2.7 GB of attention and dense weights, ~2 GB of routed experts (8 of 128 per layer), and ~0.9 GB for the LM head. At 1,469 GB/s, that gives a single-user bandwidth ceiling of ~256 tok/s. Without speculation, vLLM at 157 tok/s hits 61% of that ceiling, mostly limited by kernel launch latency across 48 visits.

Speculative decoding changes the memory math on an MoE. Verifying 8 positions together activates the union of their routed experts, reading roughly 40% of each layer's experts instead of 6%. At our measured acceptance of ~2.3 tokens per step at temperature 1.0 (per-position acceptance drops from 0.6 on the first draft to 0.33 and 0.19), the bandwidth ceiling falls to ~201 tok/s. At 190.6 tok/s, vLLM + DSpark is already at ~95% of hardware bandwidth, so further flag tuning has almost nowhere left to go. Moving past 190 tok/s would take a drafter with higher acceptance at temperature 1.0 or a verification path that touches fewer experts per layer.

Most candidate flags were unsupported, noisy, or slower:.

We also skipped rejection_sample_method: "fly" and "synthetic" on purpose because they alter the output distribution, and we wanted a strictly lossless speedup.

A few measurement challenges caught us along the way:.

Before deploying, we pinned the exact vLLM nightly digest (vllm/vllm-openai@sha256:eaa63fd6…, build 0.34.0rc1.dev1235+gf2f9edcac) and ran the acceptance gates inside a Job:.

Once those passed, we deployed the endpoint with a single hf endpoints deploy command, pinning both the image digest and model revision (authenticated access, scale-to-zero after 60 idle minutes):.

Running bench.py against the live endpoint gave 194.9 tok/s single-user, matching the Job runs once network latency is accounted for.

Sources indicate that everything from this run (PLAN.md, THEORY.md, jobs/driver.py, submit.sh, deploy.sh, and the raw ledger-*.jsonl files) is in NielsRogge/inkling-2-mini-hillclimb. To reuse the loop on another model, put your candidate and control server commands into a configs/plan-*.json file and submit it to whichever HF Jobs GPU flavor matches your target endpoint.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that most useful knowledge is written and digitized in English.
    • In a recent development, we built a small voice agent to close that gap, using CUGA as the agent harness.
    • In a recent development, A farmer asks a question aloud, in their own language: how do I tell good seed from bad?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that most useful knowledge is written and digitized in English. Most of the people who need it speak, and think, in their own regional languages like Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Gujarati, Marathi and many others. Many would rather talk than type.

    In a recent development, we built a small voice agent to close that gap, using CUGA as the agent harness. This post explains the use case and what we learned. You can try it yourself in CUGA Apps.

    In a recent development, A farmer asks a question aloud, in their own language: how do I tell good seed from bad? The agent:.

    If someone asks about cricket or coding, it politely steers them back to farming instead of making something up.

    Industry observers note that CUGA (ConfigUrable Generalist Agent) is IBM Research's open-source agent harness. It handles the model wiring, tool management, state and guardrails, so you write tools and a prompt instead of the agent loop. Here we use it as an embedded SDK inside a small web app, for three things:.

    The key design idea is simple: CUGA is a text-in, text-out brain. Voice is two thin layers around it.

    Because the agent only ever sees text, you can build and test it with plain text first, then add the ears and the mouth. You can also swap speech providers without touching the agent. We support two: Sarvam AI's cloud speech APIs, called directly from the user's browser, and open-source models (SraVaani for speech-to-text, Svara for text-to-speech) running on your own server.

    Recent findings suggest that adding speech is the easy part. The hard part is cross-lingual retrieval: a Hindi question has to find an English paragraph.

    Search works by turning text into vectors and finding the nearest ones. CUGA's default embedding model is English-only, so it turns Hindi into vectors that carry almost no meaning. With it, a Hindi or Tamil question still retrieves five passages, but they are the wrong ones. The model, correctly told to answer only from what it was given, quietly says "the handbook doesn't cover that". Every layer behaves correctly, so there is no error and no warning.

    It has been revealed that the fix is to use a multilingual embedding model (we use intfloat/multilingual-e5-large), so the same meaning lands in the same place whatever the language. Conceptually simple, though wiring it into CUGA took a small workaround (shown in the tutorial). After that, one English document serves every language, and you do not need translated copies of anything.

    Our advice: before you tune a single prompt, ask your agent one question in a non-English language and check that it finds the right pages.

    A few small decisions mattered more than we expected:.

    You do not need to set anything up to see it work. Open the voice agent in CUGA Apps on Hugging Face Spaces, ask a farming question in your language, and listen to the answer:.

    According to recent reports, want to build one yourself? Our step-by-step tutorial, Build an Indic Voice Agent with CUGA, starts from an empty folder and adds each layer in turn.

    It has been revealed that nothing here is specific to agriculture. Swap the handbook for scheme documents, health advisories, or legal guides, and you have a different assistant. Swap the speech provider and you change the deployment model, such as cloud for speed or on-premises for data sovereignty, without rewriting the agent.

    In a recent development, voice-first, multilingual assistants are how digital services can reach people who were never served well by English-only text screens. Building them on an open, auditable harness, with answers tied to sources people can check, is how they earn trust.

    It has been revealed that this approach sits precisely at the intersection of what we are building with IBM Bharat Core. Bharat Core is an optimized AI stack built on top of IBM Sovereign Core, designed specifically for the Indian ecosystem to run Indic AI workloads securely on local infrastructure. When scaling a voice agent from a prototype to a secure enterprise application (like a vernacular KYC system or multilingual government bot), you need greater control over data sovereignty. By pairing CUGA’s flexible agent harness with Bharat Core’s ready-to-deploy Indic connectors and fine-tuned models, developers can build fully compliant, sovereign AI solutions tailored to India's unique linguistic diversity.

    If you are building for India at scale, see the work happening at IBM Bharat Core.

    #115128. What happens to a long-running LangChain agent after hour 6 (measured on five stacks)

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1053 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    What happens to a long-running LangChain agent after hour 6 (measured on five stacks)

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1053 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If you run a LangChain or LangGraph agent for hours, the first thing that changes around hour 6 is probably the size of its prompt.
    • I build Argentic, an engine that keeps AI agents right for hours while prompt size is bounded.
    • Industry observers note that the shift is a bakery's operations desk.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If you run a LangChain or LangGraph agent for hours, the first thing that changes around hour 6 is probably the size of its prompt. I wanted to see what that does to the bill and to the answers, so I ran one simulated 12-hour shift through five stacks and logged every model call.

    I build Argentic, an engine that keeps AI agents right for hours while prompt size is bounded. It is one of the five stacks, and it did not win on score. The numbers are below, with versions and dates.

    Industry observers note that the shift is a bakery's operations desk. Over 12 simulated hours it has about 1,400 events: orders, price changes, stock counts, owner messages, standing instructions that get amended or revoked, and updates that contradict earlier ones. A fixed program with no model in the loop grades 663 questions about it. Every stack got the same seed, the same questions, the same grader and Claude Haiku 5.5, and each run had a spend cap.

    I ran the JavaScript packages, on 25 November 2026. Nothing was tuned. I haven't measured the Python versions.

    It has been revealed that haiku 5.5 bills a request at roughly five times the normal rate once its prompt passes 100K tokens. A loop that re-sends its history gets there eventually, and every call after that costs more.

    Deep Agents reveals it cleanly. It finished all 12 hours, and over hours 1 to 5 it spent $0.29 in total, because prompt caching is on by default and the prompt stayed under 100K. From hour 6 on it spent between $1.10 and $1.60 an hour. Its prompt grew from 5.7K tokens to 279K, and 925 of its 1,450 calls went over 100K. The whole run cost $9.46.

    It never summarised anything. Deep Agents triggers summarisation at 85% of the model's context window, and the profile LangChain gives Haiku 5.5 states that window is 1M tokens, so the trigger sits at 850K. This run never reached it. If your model has a window that large, that default means your agent keeps its whole history for a very long time, and you pay for that in the tier.

    It has been revealed that the plain LangChain loop hit its $5 cap in hour 6, at $5.09. It has no score over hours 1 to 8 because it was stopped.

    Spend is token usage at list prices, not an invoice. Over hours 1 to 8, which is 403 questions, the Agent SDK and Deep Agents scored higher than Argentic's whole range, by about 4.6 points over its mean. Letta sits at the top edge of that range, so I can't separate it from Argentic on these hours. The rivals ran once each, so their scores carry noise I haven't measured.

    It has been revealed that so on this shift, Deep Agents kept its answers right by keeping everything in the prompt, and it cost about 12.6 times what Argentic did. Argentic cost less and scored lower. Which of those matters more depends on your agent and your budget.

    According to recent reports, argentic was also worse on one kind of question: running counts, 0.86 against 0.96 for the Agent SDK. The misses I traced came down to one question about open support tickets. The agent only keeps a tally for counts that the task prompt names, and mine named stock levels but not tickets. When I resent those requests, one sentence in the task prompt fixed it: "Keep a running count of open tickets with tally: +1 when one opens, -1 when it is resolved and closed." That was a resend test, not a full run, and I didn't archive its outputs, so treat it as something to repeat.

    You need the prompt size of every call. LangChain puts it on the response message as usage_metadata. This callback writes it to a file, one line per call:.

    Pass it with config={"callbacks": [UsageLog()]} on your agent's invoke call. Check one call by hand to confirm that input_tokens includes cached tokens for your provider. Then summarise the file with jq:.

    first_over is the call number where you first crossed 100K, and 0 means you never did. Other models price long prompts differently, so check your model's price page for a step like this before you trust any estimate.

    Sources indicate that there are three common ways to do it. You can cap how much history you send, which is simple but forgets whatever you cut. You can add a summarising step, which keeps the gist but rewrites history, and details can degrade each time it runs. I didn't measure that loss here, because Deep Agents never reached its trigger. Or you can move long-lived facts out of the transcript and look them up when the agent needs them.

    Argentic takes the third route. It builds each prompt from a record of the run, under a size cap, so the prompt stays small without throwing the record away. Its largest prompt in this shift was 55K tokens, its median 37K, and none of its 1,487 calls passed 100K.

    It has been revealed that it's one seed, and the benchmark's guide asks for at least three. Only Argentic has a range, from four runs. The rivals ran once each, and three of them were stopped by spend caps before the shift ended. The rivals ran on the Anthropic API and Argentic on a local copy of the hosted engine with Haiku 5.5 through AWS Bedrock. The rivals were a few patch releases behind the newest npm versions that day.

    It has been revealed that the raw files for every run are on the page with a SHA-256 for each: the settings, the summary, every graded question, the log of every action the agent took, and every model call. https://getargentic.com/research/head-to-head/.

    Industry observers note that argentic's own engine files, meaning its prompts and internal logs, aren't published. The benchmark publishes what the shift looked like from the outside.

    It has been revealed that the benchmark, the scorer, a validator that reproduces each grade from its log, and the commands to rerun every arm are at https://github.com/open-haul/open-haul-bench (start with REPRODUCE.md). If you run it with your own setup and get different numbers, open an issue there. I'd like to see them.

    #115125. Latest Update: Where scientists draw the line on AI agents

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1691 w)
