    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Where scientists draw the line on AI agents

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1691 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that delegating research tasks to AI does not remove scientists’ responsibility for how the work is accomplished.
    • These ethical and safety questions are central to our work on AI for science.
    • To better understand what that requires, we interviewed 17 scientists working in the natural, applied, and social sciences about the responsible development of AI agents.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that delegating research tasks to AI does not remove scientists’ responsibility for how the work is accomplished. For example, a researcher using AI to review the literature needs to check whether the system overlooks conflicting evidence or makes claims the cited papers don’t support. Someone handing off data analysis to an agentic system needs to understand which methods it used, which files it accessed, and whether the results can be successfully reproduced. A researcher automating part of a lab protocol needs confidence that the system respects physical safety constraints, such as temperature limits or material toxicity, while a researcher working with human-participant data needs assurance that a system protects participants' privacy and limits who can access their information. Researchers also need clear institutional guidelines for verifying and disclosing AI-assisted work.

    These ethical and safety questions are central to our work on AI for science. Responsible science is about more than accuracy—scientific fields have ethical research norms because of past actions and choices by scientists and scientific communities, and those norms also cover how research is conducted and what impact it has. We want AI tools to expand what scientists can accomplish without compromising their ability to scrutinize evidence, verify methods, and – perhaps most importantly – stand behind their findings.

    To better understand what that requires, we interviewed 17 scientists working in the natural, applied, and social sciences about the responsible development of AI agents. These systems can use tools and carry out research tasks with varying degrees of autonomy. The interviews drew on a network of researchers established through earlier survey work—we wanted to understand how scientists would steer AI’s development to reflect the responsibilities of their fields. We asked where researchers would welcome agentic assistance, what could go wrong, and what safeguards they would need to trust agents with their own studies.

    In a recent development, our interest in these questions grew out of work to evaluate the safety of models developed at Ai2. As we expand our focus on AI for science, we’ve found that much of the safety work on scientific applications emphasizes catastrophic risks in areas such as biology and nuclear physics. We also need ways to assess whether agents follow the standards of responsible conduct of research in the fields where they’re used.

    Sources indicate that one of our main findings concerns trust. Across the interviews, we identified five dimensions of scientific trust: validation, privacy, objectivity, accountability, and transparency. Together, they reflect concerns that go beyond whether an AI system produces a correct answer. Researchers also need to understand how an answer was reached, protect sensitive information, recognize bias, and determine who is charged with verifying and standing behind AI-assisted findings. These are matters of responsible conduct of research.

    Another main finding suggests that scientists should help decide which research tasks agents take on, how those agents operate, and how their performance is evaluated. Even a technically correct result may be unsuitable for scientific use if researchers cannot inspect how it was produced, or if an agent accesses confidential data or files beyond what the researcher authorized.

    A third key finding pertains to the future of science. Interviewees were divided between excitement about AI-driven progress and existential concern about the role of human scientists. They proposed training in AI use and named developing and enforcing guidelines as a critical, timely challenge.

    In a recent development, for many participants in our interviews, the appeal of AI agents began with time-consuming research tasks—processing large datasets, writing code, documenting experimental procedures, and handling repetitive administrative work. Automating these activities could free researchers to spend more time on fieldwork, mentoring, or developing newly introduced ideas. It could also make it possible to analyze volumes of data that would be difficult to examine manually.

    But delegating research tasks creates a corresponding need to verify the work an AI system performs.

    Several participants described checking AI-generated answers against original publications rather than accepting summaries at face value. They worried about confident responses containing subtle inaccuracies, as well as tools that reinforce assumptions by retrieving only studies that support a favored hypothesis.

    In a recent development, but checking the final answer from an AI system is only part of the challenge. Researchers may also need to know which sources an agent omitted, whether it followed the requested methodology, and what information it accessed along the way.

    According to recent reports, our interviews suggest how evaluations of AI agents for scientific research could better reflect these concerns. A literature-review benchmark, for example, could test whether an agent overlooks contradictory evidence or draws conclusions unsupported by its sources. A coding benchmark could assess not only whether the generated code works, but whether the agent accesses files outside its authorized scope. Evaluations of data-processing agents could compare their methods and results with established human workflows.

    Recent findings suggest that these examples point toward a longer-term goal—a participatory benchmark in which scientists help define the research practices and safety requirements that agents should be tested against. We want to evaluate whether systems developed at Ai2 or elsewhere follow the standards of the fields where they’re used, as well as whether they complete assigned tasks.

    Industry observers note that these evaluations remain proposals to develop and test with scientists, rather than established solutions. But they offer a direction for our work at Ai2: building open scientific tools means making their behavior and limitations easier to investigate and giving the research community a role in defining what trustworthy performance looks like.

    Sources indicate that verification is only one consideration in using AI tools for science. Respondents also raised a more fundamental question—what happens to scientific expertise when AI takes over parts of the research process?

    Recent findings suggest that an early-career biologist described deliberately limiting AI use while acquiring skills they hoped to teach future students. Another researcher questioned whether producing a correct result was sufficient if the researcher learned nothing in the process: even with perfect outputs, “did the person who obtained the perfect outputs get anything out of this?”.

    It has been revealed that some participants were concerned that AI-assisted research could diminish learning, though the value of automation depends in part on the researcher and the task. An experienced scientist may reasonably delegate a familiar procedure to save time, while someone still learning that procedure may benefit from doing the work themselves.

    It has been revealed that participants also drew different boundaries around activities involving intellectual contribution. One biologist refused to use AI to generate research ideas, considering that a responsibility to retain personally. Others were more open to AI-assisted ideation or writing. An anthropologist, for example, argued that some sections of scientific papers, particularly routine descriptions of methods and results, are formulaic enough to benefit from automation.

    Even researchers who tried AI for writing sometimes reconsidered. One political scientist described using Claude to help revise a manuscript, then deciding to rewrite the entire paper because the boundaries of their own intellectual contribution had become unclear. “I don’t know what was AI and what was me,” the researcher stated.

    Recent findings suggest that context mattered, too. Having AI critique a manuscript before submission was viewed favorably by some participants, while using it to review another researcher's unpublished work raised concerns. The distinction involves more than technical capability; peer review carries responsibilities around confidentiality, attribution, and the fair evaluation of others' research.

    These disagreements suggest that responsible automation cannot be defined by a universal list of acceptable and unacceptable tasks. Scientific fields have different norms, and individual researchers may have different goals even when performing similar work.

    Industry observers note that the same tension applies to safeguards built into AI systems. One political scientist described how content restrictions that prevent AI tools from discussing certain topics could interfere with legitimate research on political violence or human rights violations. Meanwhile, participants working with sensitive human-subject data wanted stronger guarantees about privacy, access, and how information would be used.

    Both are valid concerns. An agent that acts without sufficient safeguards could expose confidential data or produce harmful results, while one that’s constrained too broadly could prevent scientists from pursuing legitimate lines of inquiry.

    This is why scientific communities need a meaningful role in shaping the boundaries of AI assistance. Developers need to understand not only which activities an agent can perform, but which decisions researchers want to retain and where safeguards are necessary—as well as where those safeguards might obstruct valuable work.

    Our findings point toward an approach to scientific AI development that starts with the people who will use the technology.

    Recent findings suggest that researchers should be able to examine an agent's contributions, determine which work to assign, and preserve opportunities to develop their own expertise. Achieving that will require technical features such as transparent records of agent actions and granular data controls, alongside evaluations informed by the standards and practices of different scientific communities.

    It will also require continued collaboration. Our study is exploratory; the findings come from interviews with 17 US-based scientists, not a representative survey of scientific opinion or an empirical evaluation of specific AI agents. Participants discussed both the generative AI tools they use today and what they anticipate from more autonomous systems. Their perspectives identify crucial concerns and design priorities, rather than establishing a consensus about how AI should be used in science.

    Industry observers note that still, they offer a path forward. At Ai2, we believe AI can accelerate scientific discovery while preserving the openness, reproducibility, and independent scrutiny that make research trustworthy. Through our broader efforts to develop and evaluate scientific agents, we aim to put those principles into practice. That means working with scientists to identify worthwhile uses for agents and translating their concerns into concrete evaluations, in addition to making it easier to understand both what these systems accomplish and how they accomplish it.

    Recent findings suggest that the promise of scientific AI isn't simply that researchers can pass off more work. It's that they can pursue questions that might otherwise be out of reach while retaining the knowledge, judgment, and agency needed to make discoveries that are their own.

    #115124. Q4_K_M vs Q5_K_M vs Q8_0: which GGUF quant should you use?

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1773 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    Q4_K_M vs Q5_K_M vs Q8_0: which GGUF quant should you use?

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1773 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Use Q4_K_M unless your memory budget clearly fits something bigger: llama.cpp's published figures put it at 4.89 bits per weight on Llama 3.1 8B and +0.1754 perplexity on Llama-3-8B, against +0.0569 for Q5_K_M and +0.0026 for Q8_0.
    • According to recent reports, the number is the bit width of most weights, the letter after it is the quantization family, and the suffix is the mix.
    • Sources indicate that the _K types are k-quants, added to llama.cpp in pull request #1684.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Use Q4_K_M unless your memory budget clearly fits something bigger: llama.cpp's published figures put it at 4.89 bits per weight on Llama 3.1 8B and +0.1754 perplexity on Llama-3-8B, against +0.0569 for Q5_K_M and +0.0026 for Q8_0. On Nodus you can test the quant on the GPU you initiative to serve it on, with an RTX 4090 listed at $0.29/hr and an A100 80 GB at $1.09/hr on the Nodus pricing page. Step up to Q5_K_M or Q6_K when the file plus your context still fits, and treat Q3 and Q2 quants as a last resort.

    According to recent reports, the number is the bit width of most weights, the letter after it is the quantization family, and the suffix is the mix. Q8_0 and Q4_0 are the older "legacy" formats. The Hugging Face GGUF docs describe them as round-to-nearest quantization in blocks of 32 weights, each block with one scale, and note they are "not used widely as of today".

    Sources indicate that the _K types are k-quants, added to llama.cpp in pull request #1684. They group weights into super-blocks of 256 and store a small scale (and for some types a minimum) per sub-block. Per the Hugging Face table, that gives the base Q4_K type 4.5 bits per weight, Q5_K 5.5, Q6_K 6.5625 and Q2_K 2.625. Q8_0 is still the common 8-bit choice because at 8 bits the simple scheme is already close to lossless.

    A file named Q4_K_M is never 4.5 bits everywhere. It is a recipe that keeps some tensors at higher precision, which is why the llama.cpp quantize README measures Q4_K_M at 4.8944 bits per weight on Llama 3.1 8B.

    It has been revealed that _S, _M and _L mean small, medium and large: how many sensitive tensors get promoted to a higher-bit type. The rules live in src/llama-quant.cpp, and they are short enough to summarize.

    In a recent development, in Q4_K_M, the attention value (attn_v) and feed-forward down projection (ffn_down) tensors are stored as Q6_K in roughly half the layers: the first eighth, the last eighth and every third layer in between. Everything else stays Q4_K.

    Q4_K_S only promotes ffn_down to Q5_K in the first eighth of layers and attn_v in the first four. Q5_K_M follows the same pattern as Q4_K_M, with Q6_K on top of a Q5_K base. _L exists only for Q3 (Q3_K_L), where it pushes those tensors to Q5_K.

    Recent findings suggest that the cost of _M over _S is small. On Llama 3.1 8B the README lists Q4_K_S at 4.36 GiB and Q4_K_M at 4.58 GiB, about 5% more. The quantize tool's own table lists the perplexity increase falling from +0.2689 to +0.1754 for that step. If you can afford the extra 0.22 GiB, take the _M.

    Sources indicate that less than most people expect down to 4 bits, and a lot below 3. The table combines the two figures llama.cpp publishes: bits per weight and file size from the README benchmark on Llama 3.1 8B, and the perplexity change listed in quantize.cpp, measured on Llama-3-8B. Perplexity is how surprised the model is by held-out text, so a bigger increase means more damage.

    Sources: llama.cpp quantize README and quantize.cpp, checked November 25, 2026.

    Damage grows slowly down to Q4_K_M, then jumps: Q2_K adds 20 times the perplexity of Q4_K_M.

    Two things stand out. Q4_0 is nearly the same size as Q4_K_S but adds 0.4685 to perplexity instead of 0.2689, so there is little reason to pick it for a upcoming file. And the curve is not linear: going from Q4_K_M to Q3_K_M saves under 0.9 bits per weight and almost quadruples the loss.

    Perplexity is one number on one model. It does not tell you how a quant handles your tool calls or your language. Treat these figures as the ranking and your own eval as the verdict.

    File size is parameters times bits per weight divided by 8. The README gives the inputs: Llama 3.1 8B is 32.1 GB at F32 (4 bytes per weight), so 32.1 / 4 = 8.03 billion weights. Llama 3.1 70B is 280.9 GB at F32, so 280.9 / 4 = 70.2 billion.

    For the 8B at Q4_K_M: 8.03B x 4.8944 / 8 = 4.91 GB. The README's 4.58 GiB is 4.92 GB, so the formula holds. For the 70B at Q4_K_M: 70.2B x 4.8944 / 8 = 42.9 GB, against 43.1 GB in the README's own memory table. The 70B mix differs slightly from the 8B one, so treat the other 70B rows as close estimates.

    A 70B at Q4_K_M is 42.9 GB, under a third of the 140.4 GB F16 file.

    The same arithmetic for the 70B gives 27.7 GB at Q2_K, 35.1 GB at Q3_K_M, 41.0 GB at Q4_K_S, 50.0 GB at Q5_K_M, 57.6 GB at Q6_K, 74.6 GB at Q8_0 and 140.4 GB at F16. For the 8B: 3.17, 4.01, 4.68, 5.72, 6.59, 8.53 and 16.06 GB.

    The file is not the whole bill, because the KV cache grows with context.

    According to recent reports, both Llama configs use 8 KV heads of 128 dimensions, with 32 layers in the 8B and 80 in the 70B. At 16 bits that is 2 x 32 x 8 x 128 x 2 = 131,072 bytes per token for the 8B and 2 x 80 x 8 x 128 x 2 = 327,680 bytes for the 70B. An 8,192-token context adds 1.07 GB and 2.68 GB respectively.

    Recent findings suggest that our rule: take the largest quant whose file plus the KV cache for your real context fits, with room left for compute buffers. If two quants fit, take the larger one. The table applies that rule at an 8,192-token context using the numbers above.

    Longer contexts shift every row down. At 32,768 tokens the 70B cache alone is 10.7 GB, which pushes a 48 GB card from Q4_K_M to Q3_K_M. For which models fit on common consumer cards, see which LLMs fit in 8, 16 or 24 GB, and for the 70B case in detail, how much VRAM a 70B model needs.

    Q4_K_M wins as the default for chat and agents on a fixed memory budget. It is under a third of F16 and the curve is still flat at that point.

    In a recent development, Q5_K_M and Q6_K win when the larger file fits with your context. They cut the perplexity increase to +0.0569 and +0.0217, a cheap upgrade if you have 1 to 2 GB to spare on an 8B.

    Q8_0 wins as the reference copy. At +0.0026 it is effectively the original model, so when a fine-tune behaves badly, compare against Q8_0 first to learn whether training or quantization caused it.

    Sources indicate that F16 or BF16 wins as the master file you quantize from. The README warns that requantizing an already-quantized file "can severely reduce quality". Keep the 16-bit GGUF and make every other quant from it.

    Speed is a smaller factor than people assume. In the README benchmark on Llama 3.1 8B, text generation ran at 71.93 tokens per second on Q4_K_M, 67.23 on Q5_K_M, 58.67 on Q6_K, 50.93 on Q8_0 and 29.17 on F16. The README does not say which machine produced these, so read them as relative.

    Smaller files usually generate faster, because generating each token means reading the weights from memory.

    In a recent development, almost always. Q2_K adds +3.5199 perplexity on Llama-3-8B, 20 times Q4_K_M, to save about 1.7 GB on an 8B. If a model only fits at Q2_K, a smaller model at Q4_K_M or Q5_K_M is usually the better trade. Q3_K_M is defensible when it is the only way a 70B fits and you have tested it on your task.

    Below 4 bits, use an importance matrix. The README says accuracy loss "can be minimized by using a suitable imatrix file", which llama-quantize takes through --imatrix.

    Industry observers note that convert once to a 16-bit GGUF, then quantize that file as many times as you like. These commands are copied from the llama.cpp quantize README:.

    Swap the last argument for Q5_K_M, Q6_K or Q8_0 to get the other files. Initiative for memory and disk: the README says the input is loaded fully into memory and gives 280.9 GB for an F32 70B. If you do not want to install anything, the README also points to the GGUF-my-repo space on Hugging Face.

    Quantizing is not where the GPU money goes. When we wrote our guide to fine-tuning a model for Ollama, llama.cpp conversion and quantization of our small test model ran on CPU only. That post covers the full export path, so we will not repeat it here.

    Sources indicate that the GPU time is in two places: training the model and checking the quant. Nodus runs fine-tunes as TrainingJobs on the cheapest capacity that will finish them, with checkpoints and recovery if a machine is lost.

    Recent findings suggest that when a Job names a 7B or 8B model, the Nodus Jobs guide sets a default memory floor of 24Gi, enough for a LoRA or QLoRA run. Checking the quant is a short Job on the hardware you will serve on: an hour on an RTX 4090 is listed at $0.29 on the Nodus pricing page, and an A100 80 GB, enough for a 70B at Q6_K with room for context, at $1.09. If the model will serve many owners rather than one, compare llama.cpp with a server built for batching in vLLM vs Ollama.

    Prices checked November 25, 2026.

    For many models it is the common default, and llama.cpp's figures show only +0.1754 perplexity on Llama-3-8B. Code and tool calling punish small errors, so if you have the memory, run your own coding eval on Q4_K_M and Q6_K and keep the smaller one only if it scores the same.

    Industry observers note that no. Q8_0 is a GGUF format for llama.cpp with one scale per 32 weights, while FP8 or bitsandbytes 8-bit are different formats for different runtimes. A Q8_0 file only loads in GGUF-compatible tools such as llama.cpp and Ollama.

    In a recent development, IQ types such as IQ4_XS (4.4597 bits per weight in the README) use an importance matrix, per the Hugging Face GGUF docs, and the family reaches down to about 2 bits. They make most sense below 4 bits. At 4 bits and above, the K-quants are the simpler default.

    It has been revealed that yes. Run the fine-tune as a TrainingJob on Nodus, download the weights it writes, merge any adapter, then convert and quantize with llama.cpp as shown above. Our Ollama export guide walks through that path.

    The Native Performance Gap: Why Your Media Tool Doesn't Need a Cloud Backend

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (514 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that every time you drop a 4K video into one of those 'free' web-based converters, you aren't just losing your privacy.
    • It has been revealed that at VanzaLabs, when we set out to build Convert & Compress, we faced a binary choice: build a thin wrapper around a Node.js backend or go native.
    • Recent findings suggest that cross-platform frameworks have their place, but they often act as a tax on your hardware’s potential.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that every time you drop a 4K video into one of those 'free' web-based converters, you aren't just losing your privacy. You are participating in a massive, inefficient data choreography. You upload 500MB of data to a server that likely lives in a different time zone, wait for a multi-tenant queue to process your request, and then download the result. It is a slow, bloated, and fundamentally flawed way to manipulate bits that already exist on the hardware in your pocket.

    It has been revealed that at VanzaLabs, when we set out to build Convert & Compress, we faced a binary choice: build a thin wrapper around a Node.js backend or go native. We chose the latter, not just for the sake of privacy, but because mobile silicon has become shockingly powerful. Modern SoCs are essentially specialized supercomputers for media encoding. When you bypass the cloud, you tap into dedicated hardware encoders (like Apple’s VideoToolbox or Android’s MediaCodec) that perform tasks in seconds which would take a generic server-side CPU significantly longer to compute.

    Recent findings suggest that cross-platform frameworks have their place, but they often act as a tax on your hardware’s potential. When you run media processing through a heavy abstraction layer, you lose the ability to fine-tune buffer management and memory allocation. In mobile development, memory is a finite, volatile resource.

    In a recent development, we treated the development of our converter like a systems-level problem. By stripping away the unnecessary networking stack, we eliminated:.

    According to recent reports, engineering for local-first means embracing the constraints of the device. When you handle HEIC to JPG conversion or 4K compression on-device, you have to write code that respects the thermal throttling of a smartphone. If you push the CPU too hard for too long, the OS kills your process.

    We optimized our pipeline by implementing granular task-batching. Instead of loading an entire batch into memory, we stream chunks. This allows us to process 50 high-resolution photos without the app crashing due to an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) error. It’s an approach that feels 'snappy' because it is essentially talking directly to the hardware's video processing unit (VPU).

    When we compared our local-only implementation to standard web-view based tools, the differences were stark:.

    There is a peculiar obsession in the industry with building 'smarter' apps that require smarter backends. But the smartest apps are often the ones that require the least infrastructure. By moving the compute to the client, we’ve effectively future-proofed the utility. The app won't stop working if our business pivots or if our API keys expire. It is a standalone, immutable tool that does exactly one thing, perfectly.

    If you are a developer looking for a reference on how to handle media without relying on server-side bloat, Convert & Compress is our proof of concept. We’ve demonstrated that you don't need a massive infrastructure budget to deliver a professional-grade media utility—you just need a deeper understanding of the metal you're running on.

    You can see our local-first implementation in action here: Download on Google Play.

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I'm building Samevia from Stepanavan, a small town in northern Armenia.
    • Today it has 460 lessons across 16 fields.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I'm building Samevia from Stepanavan, a small town in northern Armenia. It teaches whole fields of knowledge, from mathematics to psychology, as short lessons in your own language, on the web and on Android. It is free to start and works offline.

    Today it has 460 lessons across 16 fields. 429 are published in English and 269 in Armenian. Every one of them was drafted and translated by LLMs. This post is about the part that made that possible without shipping garbage: a small, boring, deterministic gate.

    In a recent development, armenian has its own alphabet. When we started translating lessons with smaller models, many outputs looked like translations to anyone who doesn't read Armenian, and were unusable to anyone who does:.

    Industry observers note that an LLM judge did not catch these reliably. A regex did.

    Every translated leaf (a heading, a paragraph, a quiz option) goes through the same checks before it is accepted:.

    If a check fails, the leaf is not "fixed up". It is sent to the next provider in the chain. Free-tier models go first; a paid model is only a backstop at the end. That ordering is why the product can be free.

    A strict gate is only useful if it rejects the right things. Two real cases from this month:.

    It has been revealed that we log every translation attempt with its outcome (ok, still_invalid, script_leak, error) and the model that produced it, and alert when the hourly success rate drops below 80%. That alert is how we noticed, yesterday, that two models in the chain had started producing mostly invalid Armenian, while others were fine. Without per-model outcomes it would have looked like "translation is flaky".

    If you read Armenian, or another language that LLMs tend to mangle, I'd value your feedback on the lessons: https://samevia.com.

    #115114. Add This Packet Of Seasoning To Pot Roast For A Delicious Southern-Style Sandwich

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (573 w)

    Add This Packet Of Seasoning To Pot Roast For A Delicious Southern-Style Sandwich

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (573 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
    • Pot roast is one of those simple homemade meals that may take a long time to cook but is pretty hands-off in the Crock Pot.
    • Ranch seasoning is basically an off-the-shelf, ready-to-go spice packet containing multiple seasonings — usually salt, onion powder, garlic powder, and other dried herbs and spices, like parsley and black pepper.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

    Pot roast is one of those simple homemade meals that may take a long time to cook but is pretty hands-off in the Crock Pot. Just brown the meat, add your ingredients, and let the cooker do its job. There are plenty of ways to upgrade a basic pot roast and some interesting regional pot roast dishes, and this simple trick is a bit of both. To give your pot roast a hint of Southern twang, add a packet of dry ranch seasoning. Similar to a set-it-and-forget-it easy French dip sandwich but Southern, a bit of ranch in your pot roast will give you some delightfully intense flavor and get you darn near a classic Mississippi pot roast.

    Ranch seasoning is basically an off-the-shelf, ready-to-go spice packet containing multiple seasonings — usually salt, onion powder, garlic powder, and other dried herbs and spices, like parsley and black pepper. Most brands also contain buttermilk and whey, which will add a bit of a creaminess factor, but you don't have to worry about the roast tasting like a bottle of ranch dressing because the mix will cook down with added beef stock and natural juices to form a nice, thick gravy. It will come out rich, bold, and savory with just a hint of tanginess from the buttermilk. Once your roast is nice and tender, you can simply slice it (or shred it) up and serve it Italian-beef or French-dip style, preferably with some melted cheese on top. The first bite through the bread into the perfectly tender and umami-rich, seasoned beef will make you a believer.

    It has been revealed that if you want to go for a more or less standard pot roast route, you can simply rub your roast with a packet of Hidden Valley Ranch Seasoning, available online and in stores, or something similar, and cook it how you normally would with beef stock, potatoes, onions, carrots, and whatever other veg you like to use. To go full-on Mississippi roast, you can forgo the veggies and slow cook it with the ranch coating, beef stock or au jus gravy mix, and a half dozen or more whole pepperoncini. Up the spice level with extra hot peppers or use the whole jar. You can even add a bit of the brine for some supplementary heat, plus a zingy kick of vinegar. This will get you closer to an actual Mississippi pot roast, which typically features mentioned peppers.

    For the bread, something that will hold up to the moisture of the roast is ideal. Toasted French bread adds a crunchy texture, but a toasted hoagie roll works great, and a thick sourdough will add a little extra tang. You'll want a cheese that melts easily, so you can swiftly broil it without overcooking the bread. A simple mozzarella is an easy, mild choice, but a nice Gruyère will bring a richer and nuttier flavor with some subtle sweetness.

    In a recent development, ranch-seasoned pot roast or the full Mississippi mix is also great on egg noodles, mashed potatoes, or rice, or you can make a simple open-faced sando with a thick Texas toast. For an even saltier, more savory roast, you can try a three-packet blend with ranch, brown gravy, and Italian-style salad dressing mixes. However, to get that good Southern flavor, don't veer too far off the ranch.

    The 9 Best Chain Restaurant BLTs, According To Customer Reviews

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2039 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A good BLT is elegantly simple, a masterclass in culinary economy.
    • These details make it hard for chain restaurants to nail a great BLT.
    • According to recent reports, cook Out has built a restaurant empire on selling comfort foods that you'd find at a backyard barbecue.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A good BLT is elegantly simple, a masterclass in culinary economy. With this sandwich, nothing is superfluous, nothing is forced. Instead, each ingredient works in unison to create an unmatched harmony of taste, temperature, and texture. Whether you're craving a light nosh or a substantial sit-down lunch, somehow a BLT always fits the bill. And because of its pared-down composition, every element has a chance to shine on its own. However, this also means there's no place to hide mistakes. If the tomato is a bit mealy, the bacon slightly chewy, or the bread a tad soft, it can throw off the entire sandwich.

    These details make it hard for chain restaurants to nail a great BLT. They serve thousands of meals every day, and each individual order exposes them to a world of criticism and critique. To save yourself from a sub-par sandwich, you need to know which chains are executing a quality BLT. And this list hopes to do just that, featuring a handful of fast food chains and restaurants that are dishing up both familiar renditions and inventive interpretations of this classic sandwich. To find the best, I searched social media, roundups, and other online forums to uncover which chain restaurants are doing the BLT justice.

    According to recent reports, cook Out has built a restaurant empire on selling comfort foods that you'd find at a backyard barbecue. From hush puppies to corn dogs to some of the best fast food milkshakes in the country. But it also offers a fun take on the classic BLT. While most people judge the sandwich's quality by the crispness of its lettuce, the juiciness of its tomato, or the number of grains in its whole wheat bread, Cook Out takes a different approach: speed, price, and efficiency.

    In a recent development, these sandwiches are essentially BLT sliders: compact handhelds you can devour swiftly and without a tummy ache. Despite their size, photos show you get a decent amount of each ingredient packed onto the tiny hamburger bun. And at a time when value is a particularly tasty quality, the fact that these mini sandwiches cost between $2 and $3.49 (depending on your location) makes them even more delicious. "They are ridiculously cheap," mentioned one customer on Facebook. "Less than two bucks..." On Reddit, the feelings are mutual, with another commenter posting, "The BLTs are the unsung hero of Cook Out." Apparently, not all heroes wear capes; some wear bacon.

    In a recent development, sonic is another chain known for its nostalgic, carhop-inspired food. It has all the munchies you crave late at night: tater tots, root beer floats, breakfast burritos — really, the menu covers the gamut. But the restaurant is best known for its selection of classics, including the BLT. While some BLTs are light and dainty, Sonic's BLT Toaster is on the heftier side, perfect if you're craving something not greasy but still substantial enough to keep you full throughout the day. The sandwich isn't such a departure from classic BLTs, but everything just feels, well, bigger. The hand-sliced tomatoes, fresh lettuce, and trio of meaty bacon strips all come sandwiched between two thick slabs of buttery Texas toast.

    In a recent development, customers, say that they love the BLT, with one YouTuber noting it's "crispy, crunchy, and yummy." And speaking of breakfast, Sonic's BLT Toaster is frustratingly elusive. It's not discontinued, but it doesn't always appear when ordering online. A workaround is to get the Grilled Cheese and just add bacon, lettuce, and tomato. Or you can just ask for it specifically if ordering in person.

    In a recent development, potbelly knows how to put together a quality sandwich, and as far as chain sub shops go, it should be in the conversation with Jersey Mike's, Jimmy John's, and Firehouse Subs — at least that's what people are saying on the Reddit threads. However, like most fast food empires, quality varies by location. Still, a good Potbelly sandwich is as solid as any, typically well-stuffed, with a great ratio of condiments and toppings.

    This same formula and attention to detail that make its Italian sub a customer favorite also show up in its BLTA (the "A" stands for avocado). Texturally, it's a terrific blend of creamy, cool, crispy, and crunchy, and unlike the more value-friendly fast food restaurants, the sandwich is assembled with a little more care. Customers note that the avocado is freshly sliced, the bread is crusty and substantial, and the pepper-crusted, applewood-smoked bacon is the best of any sandwich chain. "Potbelly makes an amazing BLT," claims one happy diner on Instagram. "...the lettuce and tomato are fresh and refreshing. The bacon is peppered, which adds a great flavor. The bread-to-ingredients ratio is amazing. Solid BLT 9/10.".

    According to recent reports, jason's Deli is more than just a deli. It has more than 200 locations, mostly in the South and Midwest, which is why it probably doesn't get the national acclaim it deserves. But Jason's makes some incredible food that's unlike anything else you'll find at other fast food restaurants and casual chains: giant baked potatoes, massive slow-cooked brisket sandwiches, and a bottomless salad bar that might just be the best in the country.

    In a recent development, its version of a BLT — aptly named the Bigger Better BLT — is no slouch, either, although it's sure to ruffle the feathers of BLT purists. Why? Well, the sandwich is stuffed with a few extra letters from the alphabet. Obviously, it includes the standard bacon, lettuce, and tomato — albeit in greater quantity than average —plus slices of avocado and a freshly cracked fried egg, all piled on two slices of multi-grain wheat. In general, customers are impressed by the amount of bacon and the overall sandwich composition. "This is my favorite menu item from here," said a Redditor after posting a glam shot of their sandwich.

    From its famous #13 Original Italian to the Big Kahuna Cheesesteak, Jersey Mike's knows how to put together a sandwich. The chain takes the same thoughtful approach with its #1 BLT. Our sister site, Chowhound, ranked it the tastiest chain restaurant BLT around, citing the quantity of ingredients and textural harmony as key reasons for its success.

    Jersey Mike's doesn't do anything special with its BLT. No bells and whistles or novel additions; it just nails the basics, with a precise ratio of tender tomato, refreshing shredded lettuce, crispy bacon, and a good mayonnaise (and some oil and vinegar or chopped pepper relish if you get it "Mike's Way"). The bread cradles the ingredients so nothing gets too soggy or, worse, falls apart.

    On a Facebook post dedicated to the BLT debate, one person commented, "Jersey Mike's is the only place I will go for 'fast food' subs!" Others agree, with another poster noting, "...this was wayyyy good [...] I only wish I got extra bacon, but there was a good amount." And while everyone appreciates a simple sandwich, many customers say their customizations improve the taste, adding everything from tangy banana peppers to spicy chipotle mayo to your standard slice of American cheese.

    Five Guys is known for its juicy burgers, thick milkshakes, and an unnecessary abundance of fries, but the fast food restaurant also makes one of the best BLTs of any national chain. However, Five Guys created some confusion among its fan base by formally "launching" the BLT sandwich just a few months ago, even though many loyal customers say it's more of a relaunch, given that it's been available for more than a decade.

    Regardless, the sandwich is now available nationwide, which is good news for anyone who loves a BLT that doesn't skimp on the B. The sandwich is served on a sesame seed burger bun, but the applewood-smoked bacon is piled so high that it's about the thickness of a double (or triple) stacked cheeseburger. "They PILE the bacon on those BLTs," commented one Redditor, "...it's unlike any BLT I've ever had because of the sheer volume of meat." Facebook users have similar feelings. Overall, customers view it as an underappreciated alternative to the major sandwich chains, especially for the price, which is a few dollars less than Five Guys' standard burger. On a Facebook post comparing BLTs from other chains, one person commented: "Should have gone to Five Guys. That's the GOAT BLT.".

    Cheba Hut has been around since 1998, with its original location satisfying hungry students from the Arizona State University campus. Its menu reflects the playful, somewhat frenzied, college-kid mentality. Sandwiches are bold and inventive, with names and ingredient combinations that would make Panera Bread blush. Its version of the BLT — the Sensi Kush — has a traditional foundation of bacon, lettuce, and tomato, but it also includes a few, dare we say, dank touches that set it apart from your other basic sandwich chain, specifically a drizzle of sriracha honey, fresh avocado, and a buttery blanket of provolone.

    Is this genius or BLT blasphemy? Based on customer reviews, it is most definitely the former. "I love a good BLT but I really love the Sensi Kush BLT from Cheba Hut! The honey sriracha sauce is 100," said one Facebook user, along with a pic of their sandwich. Customers on Instagram agree, with one commenter writing, "The sensi kush is fire," while another on Reddit said, "I love Cheba Hut! I think they make the best BLT I've ever had.".

    First Watch is a sizable chain with nearly 700 locations across mostly the eastern half of the United States. The restaurant offers a diverse lineup that emphasizes freshness and ingredient quality over speed and cost. At First Watch, there's something for everyone: lemon ricotta pancakes, power breakfast bowls, Benedicts, elaborate, lunch-y salads, etc., but when it comes to sandwiches, its BLT(E) is one of the best.

    It has been revealed that it pairs your typical BLT with two over-hard eggs (can't have messy yolks getting everything soggy) and Monterey Jack cheese — all on its artisan whole-grain bread. BLT snobs may scoff at the extra ingredients, but the bread, along with the sandwich's overall engineering, is as good as you'll find at a local cafe or diner. The portion is sizable, bordering on two portions-worth. The sandwich's flavor takes people by surprise as well, with it being filling and tasty while not weighing you down. One Instagram post noted, "I enjoyed the BLTE [...]. It was so good. [...] I think I might start orderind sandwiches at First Watch each time I go." For something even more out there, try First Watch's BLT Benedict, which is basically an open-faced BLT sandwich topped with poached eggs and hollandaise.

    In a recent development, celebrity endorsements don't mean everything, but John Oliver (the star of HBO's Last Week Tonight) once publicly stated to his friend Stephen Colbert that his favorite sandwich is none other than a Wawa BLT. But this shouldn't be such a shock. Wawa is famous for its reasonably priced subs and sandwiches, and its BLT doesn't disappoint (at least when the bacon is properly cooked). While a Tasting Table ranking didn't put the BLT at the top of the list, the author still praised the sandwich, saying it was "perfectly built...nicely slathered with creamy mayo and stuffed with strips of bacon, shredded lettuce, and sliced tomato.".

    Some chains (even a few on this list) are guilty of — every so often — skimping on ingredients. Not Wawa. Its sandwiches are pretty stuffed. One Facebook user stated, "The BLT hyperfixation is in fullllllll effect." Even if you do end up with a thin sandwich, the staff will gladly remake it to your liking. Another ordering tip: Wawa recently moved the BLT from the "cold" to "hot" sandwich section, which has caused some confusion amongst customers over fears that it had been discontinued.

    It has been revealed that to find the chain restaurants with the best BLTs that delivered on taste, price, and overall value, we dug through dozens of online forums, social media video reviews, and taste tests from within the past year. In the end, this list represents some of the best BLTs you can find, based on photos, reviews, and customer feedback.

    How I Get Free Traffic from ChatGPT in 2025 (AIO vs SEO)

    📅 04 Dec 2025 | ⏱️ 80 min read (15925 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Blogspot
