    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Calm ↗ Open Full Page

    How to lower your heart rate quickly (and keep it healthy)

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2009 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that clinically reviewed by Dr.
    • Recent findings suggest that think of your heart like a built-in dashboard for your emotions.
    • Science points to the fight-or-flight response as one of the key reasons for increased heart rate during moments of anxiety, which is simply biology doing its job, preparing you to act.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

    Recent findings suggest that think of your heart like a built-in dashboard for your emotions. When stress or worry highlights up, your pulse is often the first thing to signal it. You could be having a perfectly normal day when a terse email from your boss triggers you, and suddenly your pulse is hammering.

    Science points to the fight-or-flight response as one of the key reasons for increased heart rate during moments of anxiety, which is simply biology doing its job, preparing you to act. But when that response is triggered too often, it can leave you feeling drained and unsettled. But here’s the silver lining — learning how to lower your heart rate isn’t just about calming your body, it’s also one of the fastest ways to quiet your mind.

    According to recent reports, mind-body practices like breathwork and mindfulness are proven tools for decreasing your heart rate, giving you a natural way to reset your system in real time. By gently shifting your attention to your breath or the sensation of your feet on the ground, you’re telling your body that it doesn’t need to stay on high alert.

    Here’s why mindfulness can help with a high heart rate and how you can use it to also lessen anxiety.

    It has been revealed that oftentimes, when you feel anxious, your body activates its "fight-or-flight" response, which is controlled by the sympathetic nervous system. This response releases stress hormones like adrenaline that prepare your body to react quickly to danger (even if the threat isn’t dangerous).

    It has been revealed that as a result, your heart beats faster to pump more blood and oxygen to your muscles and brain. This is why anxiety often causes a noticeable increase in heart rate, along with sensations like pounding, racing, or skipped beats.

    This doesn’t always happen with chronic anxiety or for people with an anxiety disorder, where anxiety may exist like a constant hum in the background. In those cases, the body might feel stable until a stressor—like a missed deadline, a terse email from your boss, or a tantruming child—pushes you into a state of high stress with the body responding accordingly.

    When your heart is pounding and your thoughts are spinning, the advice to “just be present” can feel almost laughable. But mindfulness isn’t just about acting calm — it’s a practice to help teach your body that you’re safe.

    In a recent development, here’s the science: mindfulness activates the parasympathetic nervous system, the body’s natural “rest-and-digest” mode, and the biological brake to fight-or-flight. By focusing on something simple—your breath, a sound, the feeling of your feet on the floor—you send a signal that there’s no need to stay on high alert.

    Think of it less as instant chill and more as a pattern interruption. Even something small, like lengthening your exhale, can slow your heart rate and lower stress hormones. And mindfulness doesn’t require silence, stillness, or a meditation cushion. You can do it in line at the store, on a walk, or lying awake at 2am.

    The point isn’t to do it perfectly — it’s to pause and offer your body and mind a upcoming script to follow.

    When your heart’s racing and your thoughts are spiraling, it can help to have a calming practice in your back pocket that you can do any time, anywhere. And luckily, mindfulness tools are available to you no matter what situation you’re in.

    Here are 10 ways you can mindfully lower your heart rate when you’re feeling anxious.

    Industry observers note that this type of breathwork helps regulate both your breath and your heart rate. To practice, inhale for four counts, hold for four counts, exhale for four counts, and hold for four counts. Then repeat for 1–3 minutes.

    You can do this silently anywhere your anxiety strikes — at your desk, in the bathroom at a party, or while commuting.

    Related read: 10 types of breathing exercises (and how to practice them).

    Longer exhales help activate your parasympathetic nervous system. A simple pattern you can try is inhaling for four seconds and then exhaling for six or more seconds.

    Try doing this for 3–5 rounds as it can make your body feel safer and more grounded.

    Related read: Breathing for stress: 7 calming techniques that *actually* work.

    Bring yourself back into your body by naming five things you can see, four things you can touch, three things you can hear, two things you can smell, and one thing you can taste.

    This sensory awareness exercise is a gentle way to anchor yourself in the present moment, no special tools needed.

    Physical touch can be soothing, especially over your heart or stomach.

    Industry observers note that place one hand on your chest and breathe slowly. You might notice your heart beating fast at first, but stay with it. That awareness typically fades as your body settles into it.

    Give yourself permission to do nothing for a full minute. Just breathe and be still.

    You could even say a simple phrase to yourself, like “I am here” or “This moment is enough,” to help anchor your focus.

    💙 Take a moment to rest and reset by listening to The Pause with Jeff Warren.

    Light movement can help discharge anxious energy.

    You might try going for a short walk, stretching your arms overhead, rolling your shoulders slowly, or shaking out your hands.

    Read more: 7 simple movement exercises to boost your mental health.

    Shifting your posture, especially uncrossing your legs and relaxing your shoulders, can help reset your nervous system.

    If you’ve been sitting or lying down, stand up and stretch. If you’ve been standing, try sitting with your feet firmly planted.

    To help regulate your nervous system, picture yourself somewhere safe or peaceful, using all of your senses.

    Ask yourself what the air smells like, what you can hear, and feel the imaginary ground beneath your feet.

    In a recent development, if you’re feeling hot or flushed from anxiety, hold something cold like a drink or a frozen pack. You could also splash your face with cool water.

    This can help slow your heart rate through a mechanism called the mammalian dive reflex.

    Validation can calm your inner critic and help you move through anxiety with more self-compassion.

    The next time you feel your heart racing, say to yourself, “I’m noticing my heart’s beating fast, and that’s okay,” or “I’ve felt this before, and it passed. It’ll pass again.”.

    💙 Keep your inner critic at bay by listening to Tara Brach’s Radical Self-Compassion series.

    The tips above are for moments when your heart is racing. Your resting heart rate is a longer game. It's your pulse when you're calm and still, and it may shift over weeks or months with regular habits.

    In a recent development, many people check it first thing in the morning, before getting out of bed. Tracking it for a few weeks may show you your own pattern. For most adults, a normal resting rate falls between 60 and 100 beats per minute. If yours is often above that range or changes suddenly, it may be worth talking to a healthcare provider. The habits below may be worth trying, so pick the ones that fit your life right now.

    Industry observers note that regular movement: Endurance activity, such as brisk walking or cycling, and yoga have both been linked to a lower resting heart rate in healthy people. U.S. guidelines suggest at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, and shorter bouts count toward that total.

    Sources indicate that consistent sleep: Short or broken sleep is linked to more activity in the body's stress systems, which may nudge your heart rate up. Sleep experts suggest most adults get at least seven hours a night on a regular basis, though your own needs may differ. If you're curious how your heart rate behaves overnight, here's what to know about your sleeping heart rate.

    Stress management: One review of 45 trials found that meditation was linked to a lower heart rate. A regular mindfulness practice, even a few minutes a day, may be a place to start.

    In a recent development, nicotine: Nicotine may raise your heart rate for a while after each use. If you'd like to cut back, a healthcare provider can help.

    💙 Meditation may also support your heart over time. Here are five ways to try it.

    Recent findings suggest that get emergency care right away if your racing heart comes with chest pain, fainting, or signs of heart failure, such as swelling in your legs. Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room.

    Industry observers note that for a racing heart without those signs, it may be worth booking a visit if it keeps coming back. A closer look may be especially helpful if it disrupts your sleep, or if you have heart disease or a family history of heart rhythm problems.

    A doctor may start by checking your heart rhythm with an ECG, a quick test that records your heart's electrical activity. If they find no heart problem, stress or anxiety may be behind it, and the tips above may help.

    Industry observers note that many times, it can feel like your heart is racing for no reason. But your body could be reacting to subtle stress signals or low-lying anxiety. Poor sleep, dehydration, low blood sugar, and even scrolling through overwhelming news can all tell your nervous system to go into high alert.

    Sources indicate that it can also happen when your system’s on edge, and as a result, it doesn’t take much to push it over. When this happens, it is usually just your body trying to protect you.

    Mindfulness can help lower your heart rate. Techniques like breathwork, grounding, and body scans have been shown to activate your parasympathetic nervous system, which slows your heart rate and helps regulate stress responses.

    Sources indicate that practicing mindfulness can be as simple as noticing your feet on the ground or taking a few deep breaths after you brush your teeth. Little moments like this can help remind your body that it’s not in danger.

    A good way to decrease your heart rate is to slow your breathing, especially your exhale. This signals safety to your nervous system. Other useful tools are:.

    Practicing the 5–4–3–2–1 technique by naming five things you can see, four things you can touch, three things you can hear, two things you can smell, and one thing you can taste.

    Placing a hand over your chest to create a sense of connection and calm.

    Changing your body position by uncrossing your legs and relaxing your shoulders.

    Getting some fresh air by going for a brief walk.

    Engaging your senses by holding something cold.

    Anxiety and elevated heart rate often reinforce each other. This is because when your brain senses a threat, your heart races. Then your racing heart convinces your brain that something must be wrong. But the good news is that lowering your heart rate can help disrupt this cycle.

    Industry observers note that some ways to do this are slowing your breathing, moving gently, and bringing your attention back to your body. All of these actions can create just enough space for your thoughts to soften.

    An occasional spike during rest, especially when you’re anxious or overtired, is usually not dangerous. But if your resting heart rate is consistently elevated, it could be worth talking to a healthcare provider. Chronic stress, certain medications, and underlying conditions could be playing a role.

    With that remarked, bodies do fluctuate. So pay more attention to the broader pattern of how often it happens and what might be triggering it.

    ADHD Medications May Improve Brain Fog in Perimenopausal Women: Upcoming Research

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1314 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Additudemag

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Preliminary evidence shows self-reported brain fog decreases and executive function improves in perimenopausal women treated with ADHD medications.
    • Industry observers note that stimulant and non-stimulant medications used to treat ADHD significantly improve self-reported executive dysfunction in perimenopausal women without ADHD, according to preliminary evidence presented at the annual meeting of The Menopause Society last month in San Diego.
    • Recent findings suggest that during the presentation titled “Brain Fog or ADHD?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Preliminary evidence shows self-reported brain fog decreases and executive function improves in perimenopausal women treated with ADHD medications.

    Industry observers note that stimulant and non-stimulant medications used to treat ADHD significantly improve self-reported executive dysfunction in perimenopausal women without ADHD, according to preliminary evidence presented at the annual meeting of The Menopause Society last month in San Diego. (These findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.)1.

    Recent findings suggest that during the presentation titled “Brain Fog or ADHD? Executive Dysfunction in Perimenopause: A Scoping Review of the Role of ADHD Medications,” researchers discussed the effectiveness of two ADHD medications: lisdexamphetamine (brand name: Vyvanse), a stimulant, and atomoxetine, a non-stimulant. They studied the impact of these medications on cognition and ADHD symptom severity in women aged 45 to 60 years during the perimenopausal period. The systematic review included three crossover randomized controlled trials involving 60 patients and two cross-sectional studies of 6,048 patients from Iceland and the U.K.

    According to recent reports, the study found that both lisdexamphetamine (LDX) and atomoxetine (ATX) significantly improve self-reported executive dysfunction, as measured by the Brown Attention Deficit Disorder Scale (BADDS), a self-report rating scale that measures ADHD symptoms, compared to placebo. The BADDS scores for LDX users dropped from 35.7 to 21.2, compared to 29.8 with placebo. The BADDS scores for ATX users fell from 38.6 to 25.5, compared to 30.1 with placebo. Neuroimaging data from a subset of women taking LDX further supports these findings.

    During perimenopause, declining or fluctuating estrogen levels affect dopamine and norepinephrine signaling in the prefrontal cortex of the brain. As a result, many perimenopausal women experience “brain fog,” which is an umbrella term for forgetfulness, slow thinking, difficulty finding words, and reduced concentration, which can also be a symptom of ADHD. This overlap often leaves clinicians trying to discern whether a patient’s brain fog stems from hormonal fluctuations or undiagnosed ADHD, or both.

    “Many women at perimenopause notice changes in focus, memory, and organization that look a lot like ADHD, and the two can be hard to tell apart,” stated lead author Jennifer Tat, M.D. candidate and fourth-year medical student at the University of Tennessee Health Science Center in Memphis.

    In an ADDitude survey of more than 5,000 women with diagnosed and undiagnosed ADHD, 94% of survey respondents said their ADHD symptoms grew more severe during perimenopause and menopause. During this stage, respondents said the most impactful ADHD symptoms were brain fog or memory concerns, and overwhelm, both of which 70% of women said had a “life-altering impact” in their 40s and 50s.

    According to recent reports, “Brain fog became unmanageable,” wrote one 45-year-old mother of two who entered perimenopause at age 41. “Distractibility increased and my inability to complete work tasks in an appropriate amount of time decreased. I began spending all night working just to keep up. Things that I used to have unconscious strategies to deal with were no longer manageable.”.

    “I never experienced rage or brain fog before perimenopause,” wrote one woman. “Overwhelm has been more frequent in recent years, and depression began in my 40s. I definitely attribute some of this to hormonal changes.”.

    Sources indicate that “In perimenopause, the brain fog and memory, inattention, distractibility, perfectionism, hyperactivity, and restlessness issues become progressively worse,” wrote a 52-year-old woman diagnosed with ADHD at age 50. “I have always had these symptoms, but I was able to manage them with systems that I created for myself. My ability to manage them has declined significantly, and this makes these symptoms seem like they are the worst they have ever been.”.

    While preliminary evidence from the systematic review found ADHD medications improve subjective executive function, the medications had little to no significant impact on objective cognitive measures, according to tests measuring working memory and sustained attention.

    Prior research suggests otherwise.

    In the ADDitude article “Could ADHD Medications Improve Memory, Focus & Organization in Menopausal Women? The Research Says Yes,” the late Thomas E. Brown, Ph.D., described how his research with C. Neill Epperson, M.D., found ADHD medications alleviated cognitive problems resembling ADHD symptoms in menopausal women without ADHD.

    The series of three studies measured symptoms with BADDS, which Brown developed. The first study found that ATX treatment significantly improved BADDS scores for working memory; focus scores improved in BADDS scores for women treated with ATX.2 In the second study, executive functions improved, including an objective measure of short-term working memory, in 41% of menopausal women taking 20 to 60 mg LDX daily, compared to 17% for the women on the placebo.3 The third study examined the effects of LDX on the brain functioning of women with no history of ADHD, but with reported cognitive difficulties with working memory, organization, focus, and attention that had begun during menopause.4.

    According to recent reports, “As predicted, neuroimaging data demonstrated that LDX activated executive networks in specific areas of the brain,” Brown wrote. “Those data also showed that LDX’s effect on specific brain regions was associated with improved BADDS scores overall, and with BADDS scores for activation and alertness/effort. Imaging data indicated that improvements in brain activation were significantly larger when women were on LDX than when they were on placebo.”.

    The studies were published in peer-reviewed medical journals in 2011, 2015, and 2017; however, Brown wrote in 2021, “results of that research have not yet been widely recognized.”.

    There is currently no FDA-approved pharmacological intervention for executive dysfunction and brain fog during perimenopause or menopause. Research on the most effective treatments for ADHD during perimenopause is limited as well. That stated, Patricia Quinn, M.D., explained during a 2026 ADDitude webinar that available data and observational evidence suggest that many women could benefit from estrogen supplementation and increased stimulant dosages during this phase.

    “Perimenopause is when you need the most help, the most support,” Quinn stated in her webinar, “Perimenopause in Women with ADHD.” “Estrogen… makes your stimulant more effective.”.

    One roadblock to care is the fact that many healthcare professionals are ill-equipped to provide responsive, coordinated, evidence-based treatment and support to help women navigate menopause, according to a study published in The Lancet Obstetrics, Gynecology, & Women’s Health. The 2026 study cited inadequate medical training, paltry research, and persistent gaps in knowledge as reasons for the “fragmented care.”5.

    Combined, these preliminary findings could open the door to a nonhormone therapeutic option for addressing perimenopausal executive dysfunction, according to researcher Tat.

    It has been revealed that “Our review found early signs that ADHD medications may help women feel more on top of their daily lives,” Tat stated. “While it’s too early to recommend these medications, a quick screen for ADHD symptoms is a simple step that could help women get the right care.”.

    How to reduce screen time and improve your digital well-being

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1394 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that once a week, your phone sends you a screen time report.
    • In a recent development, screen time adds up fast when work emails and news alerts share a device with your group chats and favorite shows.
    • It has been revealed that conventional wisdom might say “just put the phone down.” But you don’t have to completely give up screens to feel more in control of how you use them.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

    Recent findings suggest that once a week, your phone sends you a screen time report. You wince at the number, then swipe it away with the same thumb you were scrolling with.

    In a recent development, screen time adds up fast when work emails and news alerts share a device with your group chats and favorite shows. By evening, you can feel worn out even if the day wasn’t particularly busy.

    It has been revealed that conventional wisdom might say “just put the phone down.” But you don’t have to completely give up screens to feel more in control of how you use them. A few small tweaks to your daily routine are a good place to start. Below, you’ll find some realistic ways to cut back, plus a look at why it can feel so hard to put your phone down.

    Sources indicate that there's no set amount of time that counts as too much. What matters more is how your screen use affects you. Signs worth noticing include strained eyes, restless sleep, reaching for your phone out of habit, and feeling worse after scrolling. If any of these sound familiar, the tips below may help.

    Recent findings suggest that 💙 Not sure if this sounds like you? Check out these five signs you might be online too much.

    It has been revealed that if “one more video” keeps turning into one more hour, you’re in good organization. Many apps are designed to keep you scrolling, so you’ll need more than willpower to cut back. Start with one or two tips that feel doable right now. You can come back to the rest later.

    It has been revealed that bright colors can make apps harder to put down, and notification badges and thumbnails are built to draw you in. Switching your screen to black and white takes away some of that appeal, which can make scrolling feel less rewarding.

    Try: Search “grayscale” or “color filters” in your phone’s settings. You’ll usually find it under Accessibility or Well-Being.

    Industry observers note that grayscale may look odd for a day or two. Some people keep it on all day, and others only turn it on in the evening to wind down. You can turn it off whenever you need to, like when you’re using maps or looking at photos.

    💙 Listen to the Build Healthier Phone Habits series with Dr. Aditi Nerurkar on Calm.

    Time can slip by while you scroll. Set a daily limit on your one or two most-used apps, and your phone will nudge you when you reach it.

    Try: Search “app limits” or “app timers” in your phone’s settings. You’ll usually find it under screen time.

    Start with a limit slightly below how much you use those apps now, then lower it gradually. Smaller steps are often more sustainable than cutting back all at once.

    Sources indicate that notifications like news alerts, app promos, social likes, and game reminders mostly add noise. Keep the ones you rely on, such as texts, calls, and reminders, and turn off the rest.

    Try: Search “notifications” in your device settings, then toggle off the alerts you don’t need, starting with the apps that send the most.

    Constant check-ins can keep you glued to your screens all day. Pick a few set times to go through your messages, emails, and feeds.

    Try: Limit your check-ins to lunchtime and after work, and keep your personal devices out of reach in between.

    Before you open your phone, take one slow breath and ask yourself why you’re reaching for it. If the answer is just habit, that brief pause may be enough to snap you out of autopilot.

    Try: Breathe in for four counts and out for six, then see if you still want to unlock your phone.

    💙 Discover 10 types of breathing exercises you can try anytime, anywhere.

    When you feel the urge to pick up your phone, try turning to an offline activity instead. Keep an activity you enjoy within reach, like a book on the couch or a sketchpad on the table.

    💙 Want to work on the habit before the urge hits? Explore Tame Your Scrolling Habit with Rose Nisker on Calm.

    Industry observers note that choose one or two spots to keep screen-free, such as the dinner table or your bedroom. A clear boundary often works better than a vague promise to use screens less. These zones also give you room to be more present, like during a family meal or your evening wind-down.

    Sources indicate that try: Place your phone in a dedicated spot, like a basket by the door. If you share a home, invite everyone to join.

    💙 Not ready to go phone-free at night? Tune in to Sleeping with Your Phone with Dr. Matthew Walker on Calm.

    Pick a cutoff time for all your screens, such as 30 minutes before bed, and stick to it as best you can. Late-night screen use can keep your mind active and make it harder to fall asleep.

    If you usually watch a TV show before bed, choose one episode and turn off autoplay.

    Try: Schedule a nightly reminder for your cutoff. Swap your screen time for a calming activity, like journaling or a short meditation.

    💙 Press play on the Wind Down (for Sleep) meditation on Calm.

    A few common app features can keep you hooked:.

    Infinite scroll: Newly introduced posts keep loading, so you never reach a natural stopping point.

    Autoplay: The next video or episode starts on its own, which keeps you watching unless you stop it.

    Unpredictable notifications: Each message or like feels like a small reward, and not knowing when the next one will pop up keeps you checking.

    Your emotions play a part too. A screen can be a quick escape when you’re stressed or putting something off. It can bring relief in the moment, even if you feel more drained afterward.

    💙 If your screen time has been weighing on your mood, read our guide on what to do if technology is impacting your mental health.

    If you want to cut back on screen time without giving up after a few days, start small. Choose one change, like keeping your phone off the dinner table, and give yourself time to adjust before you make another tweak to your routine. If you slip back into old habits, you can always start again the next day.

    Industry observers note that to set screen time limits that stick, build them into your routine so you don’t have to rely on willpower in the moment. You could use an app timer or set aside a screen-free time each day, like the first half hour after you wake up.

    Industry observers note that there isn’t a daily screen time limit that works for every adult. If you’d like to use screens less, a good starting point is a limit slightly below your current daily average, and you can lower that limit gradually as you get used to it.

    Recent findings suggest that how you spend your screen time matters just as much. An hour on a video call with a friend often leaves you feeling better than an hour of doomscrolling.

    It has been revealed that you can reduce your screen time at night by setting a cutoff time before bed and charging your phone across the room. Swap your late-night scroll for a book or a short meditation to help you relax before sleep.

    To help your family reduce screen time together, make it a shared blueprint. You could agree on screen-free times, such as during meals or the first hour after school or work. Try leading by example, rather than telling your kids or partner what to do.

    In a recent development, no, you don’t have to quit screens completely to feel better. Technology connects you to the people and things you care about. You can cut back on the screen use that leaves you feeling worse, like aimless scrolling, and keep what you value.

    Mental health is hard. Getting support doesn't have to be. The Calm app puts the tools to feel better in your back pocket, with personalized content to manage stress and anxiety, get better sleep, and feel more present in your life.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.
    • Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.
    • People who drink diet soft drinks can keep weight off for two years about as well as those who drink water.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.

    Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.

    People who drink diet soft drinks can keep weight off for two years about as well as those who drink water.

    Among those who completed the trial, average weight loss was 4.8 kg in the diet drink group and 3.7 kg in the water group (which was not a statistically significant difference).

    Both groups took part in a weight management programme and remained lighter a year after regular support ended.

    They also reported similar changes in hunger, despite the difference in how sweet their drinks tasted.

    Almost 500 adults with overweight or obesity began the trial after being randomly assigned to drink water or commercially available diet drinks each day.

    The study included regular diet drink consumers alongside those who rarely or never chose them.

    Everyone began with 12 weeks of active weight loss, followed by 40 weeks of support to help them maintain their progress.

    Sugar intake fell by similar amounts in both groups.

    One theory is that people learn to expect energy when they taste something sweet.

    If the expected calories fail to arrive, the theory goes, that mismatch might affect hunger and lead people to make up the difference by eating more later.

    Comparing water with a diet soft drink allows researchers to ask whether sweet taste matters during weight management, since both drinks provide little or no energy.

    By the end of the trial, hunger ratings had risen slightly in both groups, and the change was similar whether participants drank water or diet drinks.

    Professor Joanne Harrold, the study’s first author, stated:.

    “These latest findings show that concerns about sweeteners disrupting appetite or causing weight gain are not supported when tested in a rigorous, long-term randomised trial.”.

    When water or a diet drink replaces a sugary soft drink, the swap also cuts the calories in that serving.

    A review of 17 randomised trials found small reductions in body weight when people replaced sugary drinks with low- or no-calorie sweetened alternatives, with results broadly similar to those for water (McGlynn et al., 2022).

    The two-year trial adds a longer view of what happens when people keep the sweet taste in their drinks while working to maintain weight loss.

    The study was published in the British Journal of Nutrition (Harrold et al., 2026).

    Exploring non-stimulant ADHD treatment? Use these questions to guide your next doctor discussion.

    Navigating Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) treatment options as an adult can feel overwhelming, but finding a treatment proposal that aligns with your specific health goals is an important first step. ADHD treatment isn’t one-size-fits-all. Non-stimulant treatments offer an option without controlled-substance management.

    In a recent development, finding a treatment is a collaborative process. My role as a healthcare provider is to provide education and guidance to help patients make informed decisions about their care. As you explore whether non-stimulant options are the right fit for your daily routine, having clear, open communication is essential. To help guide a thoughtful, personalized conversation at your next doctor’s appointment, I’ve put together a list of key questions to help you get started. Dr. Jo Hughes is a paid consultant compensated by Supernus.

    Non-stimulants are noncontrolled prescription medications used to treat the core ADHD symptoms, inattention, hyperactivity, and/or impulsivity.

    With consistent daily dosing, non-stimulant medications can provide continuous medication exposure over a 24-hour period.

    Most non-stimulant medications offer a distinct and targeted approach to help manage daily ADHD symptoms, working gradually over time to improve symptom control.

    Every non-stimulant ADHD medication has a different safety profile, so side effects can vary. Having an open conversation with your provider before starting treatment is the best way to ensure your initiative fits your needs and daily routine.

    Recent findings suggest that non-stimulants are noncontrolled medications. Talk to your doctor about prescription and refill options, including whether telehealth appointments are appropriate for you.

    Qelbree® (viloxazine extended-release capsules) is a convenient once-a-day non-stimulant ADHD medication for adults and kids ages 6 years and older. It was the first non-stimulant ADHD medication approved in over a decade with approximately 3 million prescriptions filled since launch in 2021 (for children 6-17 years old) and 2022 (in adults 18 years and older).

    Industry observers note that qelbree® (viloxazine extended-release capsules) is a prescription medicine used to treat ADHD in adults and children 6 years and older. Please click here for full Prescribing Information, including Boxed Warning, and Medication Guide.

    Qelbree may increase suicidal thoughts and actions in children and adults with ADHD, especially within the first few months of treatment or when the dose is changed. Tell your doctor if you or your child have (or if there is a family history of) suicidal thoughts or actions before starting Qelbree. Monitor your or your child’s moods, behaviors, thoughts, and feelings during treatment with Qelbree. Report any latest or sudden changes in these symptoms right away.

    See below for full Important Safety Information.

    Beyond its established presence, Qelbree offers treatment versatility for patients with ADHD in a number of ways:.

    Air Pollution Reprograms Brain Immune Cells, Raises Dementia Risk by 25%

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1023 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, A new study reveals that fine particulate air pollution (PM2.5) raises dementia risk by 25% and triggers Alzheimer’s-like brain damage even without amyloid plaques.
    • According to recent reports, microscopic soot, industrial emissions, and wildfire smoke, collectively categorized as fine particulate matter 2.5 (PM2.5), have long been recognized as major drivers of cardiovascular and respiratory disease.
    • Now, a comprehensive translational study published in the Journal of Neuroinflammation by researchers at Case Western Reserve University, University Hospitals, and the Louis Stokes Cleveland VA Medical Center provides compelling human and experimental evidence that air pollution directly fuels neurodegeneration by hijacking the brain’s immune system.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, A new study reveals that fine particulate air pollution (PM2.5) raises dementia risk by 25% and triggers Alzheimer’s-like brain damage even without amyloid plaques. The research highlights that inhaled pollution reprograms the brain’s resident immune cells (microglia), compromises the blood-brain barrier, drains cellular energy reserves, and kills newborn neurons in the hippocampus.

    Source: Case Western Reserve University.

    According to recent reports, microscopic soot, industrial emissions, and wildfire smoke, collectively categorized as fine particulate matter 2.5 (PM2.5), have long been recognized as major drivers of cardiovascular and respiratory disease. Mounting epidemiological evidence has also linked polluted air to cognitive decline, yet whether inhaled particles actively cause dementia, and precisely how they injure the brain, has remained an urgent scientific question.

    Now, a comprehensive translational study published in the Journal of Neuroinflammation by researchers at Case Western Reserve University, University Hospitals, and the Louis Stokes Cleveland VA Medical Center provides compelling human and experimental evidence that air pollution directly fuels neurodegeneration by hijacking the brain’s immune system.

    Led by co-senior authors Dr. Sanjay Rajagopalan and Dr. Andrew Pieper, the research team combined population-scale human health tracking with controlled five-month inhalation experiments in mice to map the cellular chain reaction linking dirty air to dementia.

    To quantify how long-term air pollution exposure shapes dementia risk across diverse genetic backgrounds, the researchers analyzed medical and environmental records from roughly 500,000 adults enrolled in the UK Biobank, tracked for up to 14 years.

    According to recent reports, even after controlling for confounding variables, including age, smoking status, diabetes, and socioeconomic factors—people residing in the most polluted third of geographic regions were 25% more likely to develop Alzheimer’s disease or a related dementia than those living in the cleanest third. Crucially, high air pollution elevated dementia risk regardless of whether an individual carried high or low inherited genetic risk for Alzheimer’s.

    To test causation directly, the investigators exposed mice to real-world outdoor Cleveland air for five months, concentrating PM2.5 particles to match levels recorded in the world’s most heavily polluted urban centers.

    Even in otherwise healthy mice without genetic predispositions to neurodegeneration, chronic PM2.5 exposure triggered widespread brain pathology:.

    In a recent development, remarkably, these memory deficits and Alzheimer’s-like cellular injuries emerged in healthy mice completely devoid of amyloid plaques. When the researchers exposed mice genetically engineered to develop Alzheimer’s pathology to the same polluted air, the particles inflicted identical neuroinflammatory and metabolic damage while simultaneously accelerating amyloid plaque accumulation.

    In a recent development, “By recreating in mice what happens when people breathe polluted air, we found that pollution causes major changes in which genes are active in the brain’s immune cells,” explained Rajagopalan, professor of medicine and director of the Cardiovascular Research Institute at Case Western Reserve School of Medicine. “These cells normally keep the brain healthy by clearing away debris and fighting infection. Seeing how pollution disrupts them helps explain how a stress that affects much of the world’s population harms the brain, and it points us toward a way to treat it.”.

    In a recent development, “We’ve identified a key way that air pollution harms the healthy brain and speeds up Alzheimer’s disease,” added Pieper, director of the Harrington Discovery Institute Brain Health Medicines Center and psychiatrist at the Louis Stokes Cleveland VA Medical Center. “This helps us understand how factors in our environment can accelerate and intensify brain diseases of aging. It also opens the door to studying other environmental stresses on the brain, and to finding ways to keep the brain resilient even when we can’t avoid those stressors.”.

    How much does air pollution increase the risk of developing dementia?

    In an analysis of nearly 500,000 adults tracked for up to 14 years, researchers found that people living in areas with the highest levels of fine particulate air pollution were 25% more likely to develop Alzheimer’s disease or related dementias than those in the cleanest areas, even among people with low genetic risk.

    What does fine particulate air pollution (PM2.5) physically do to the brain?

    In mouse experiments recreating urban air pollution, inhaled PM2.5 particles caused the blood-brain barrier to leak, triggered brain inflammation, lowered cellular energy reserves (NAD+/NADH ratio), killed newborn memory neurons in the hippocampus, and reprogrammed the genes of the brain’s immune cells (microglia).

    Does air pollution only harm brains that already have Alzheimer’s plaques?

    No. Researchers were struck to find that air pollution caused memory problems, immune cell disruption, and neuron death in healthy mice that had no amyloid plaques at all, while also speeding up plaque buildup in mice genetically prone to Alzheimer’s disease.

    Air pollution exposure interacts with Alzheimer’s genetic susceptibility to reshape microglial epigenomic and transcriptional programs.

    In a recent development, chronic exposure to fine particulate matter air pollution (PM2.5) is associated with cognitive decline and neurodegenerative disease, but the biology connecting inhaled particles to the brain remains incompletely defined. Among 475,325 eligible UK Biobank participants, long-term PM2.5 exposure and Alzheimer disease (AD) polygenic risk were both independently associated with higher risk of AD and related dementias (ADRD).

    The PM2.5-by-polygenic risk score (PRS) interaction in Cox models was statistically significant but sub-multiplicative or below unity (interaction HR 0.981, 95% CI 0.965–0.998; p = 0.026), indicating that the combined association was smaller than the simple product of the two individual associations.

    To define the underlying biology, we exposed 5xFAD mice, an amyloid-based model of AD, and wild-type (WT) littermates to concentrated ambient PM2.5 or filtered air for 20 weeks. PM2.5 exposure activated microglia, disrupted the blood-brain barrier, depleted the brain NAD+/NADH pool required for resilience and repair, impaired postnatal hippocampal neurogenesis, and caused cognitive deficits.

    In 5xFAD mice it additionally increased amyloid burden. Paired RNA-seq and ATAC-seq of microglia isolated from the same animals showed that exposure remodeled both gene expression and chromatin accessibility, and that that magnitude and direction of this response depended on genotype, converging on inflammatory, lysosomal, oxidative-stress, synaptic, and amyloid-related pathways.​.

    ​These population-scale data in humans and experimental data in mice​ support PM2.5 as an environmental neurotoxicant and define microglial regulatory programs through which genetic background shapes the biological response to a common and modifiable exposure.

    Brain Speech Hub Builds a “Blueprint” Before We Speak

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1502 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, neuroscientists have overturned a century-old textbook model of human language, revealing that a key speech comprehension region inside Wernicke’s area also generates an abstract “blueprint” for upcoming words a quarter-second before we speak.
    • For more than a century, neuroscience textbooks have divided human language into two separate anatomical compartments: Wernicke’s area in the temporal lobe to understand heard speech, and frontal motor circuits (such as Broca’s area and the motor cortex) to produce spoken words.
    • Yet that neat division never fully explained a persistent clinical paradox: why patients who suffer strokes or injuries in Wernicke’s area frequently struggle not only to comprehend language, but also to retrieve and speak the words they intend to say.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, neuroscientists have overturned a century-old textbook model of human language, revealing that a key speech comprehension region inside Wernicke’s area also generates an abstract “blueprint” for upcoming words a quarter-second before we speak. The study shows that listening and speaking neurons sit side by side, opening new targets for neurosurgical mapping, autism research, and brain-computer interfaces that restore speech.

    For more than a century, neuroscience textbooks have divided human language into two separate anatomical compartments: Wernicke’s area in the temporal lobe to understand heard speech, and frontal motor circuits (such as Broca’s area and the motor cortex) to produce spoken words.

    Yet that neat division never fully explained a persistent clinical paradox: why patients who suffer strokes or injuries in Wernicke’s area frequently struggle not only to comprehend language, but also to retrieve and speak the words they intend to say.

    In a recent development, now, in a landmark study published in Science, researchers at UC San Francisco (UCSF) led by neurosurgeon Dr. Edward Chang have resolved that 150-year-old puzzle.

    Drawing on 15 years of high-resolution intracranial brain recordings alongside targeted neural experiments, the team demonstrated that a specialized hub within Wernicke’s area actively generates a cognitive “blueprint” for each word roughly a quarter-second before a person begins to speak.

    Recent findings suggest that in the 1870s, German neurologist Carl Wernicke originally speculated that the posterior temporal lobe housed an “auditory image of words”, an internal template that could guide spoken output. Over subsequent decades, however, because the region sits nestled inside auditory cortex, neuroscientists largely pigeonholed it as purely a passive receiver for incoming speech sounds.

    Recent findings suggest that “What’s different now is that we finally have the tools and the data to see the brain at the speed and scale at which speech actually happens — millisecond by millisecond, down to individual neurons,” explained co-first author Dr. Matthew Leonard, associate professor of neurological surgery at UCSF.

    Combining longitudinal intracranial recordings gathered in Chang’s laboratory with fresh experiments designed to separate listening from speaking, Leonard and co-first author Dr. Alex Silva, a student in UCSF’s Medical Scientist Training Program, pinpointed a crucial cortical hub: the left posterior superior temporal gyrus (lpSTG).

    Tracking neural activity at millisecond resolution revealed that specific populations of neurons inside the lpSTG surged into action approximately 250 milliseconds (a quarter-second) before vocalization began.

    Industry observers note that crucially, this pre-speech firing did not represent raw acoustic sounds or physical movements of the lips and tongue. Instead, lpSTG neurons constructed an abstract linguistic blueprint encoding:.

    Once assembled in the lpSTG, this structural blueprint traveled forward to speech-planning networks in the frontal lobe, and subsequently to the motor cortex, which translated the initiative into precise articulatory muscle commands. Furthermore, high-resolution mapping showed that neurons dedicated to hearing speech sit directly beside, and sometimes overlap with, the neurons generating outgoing word blueprints.

    Sources indicate that “This changes the textbook view of how the brain perceives and produces speech,” mentioned Chang, chair of the UCSF Department of Neurological Surgery and member of the UCSF Weill Institute for Neurosciences. “Instead of being separate systems, the processes of hearing speech and actually speaking are very intertwined.”.

    Sources indicate that housing incoming auditory processing and outgoing word planning inside the same microcircuit provides a compelling neural mechanism for how infants acquire language, converting heard sounds directly into motor-ready speech blueprints. It also offers a targeted anatomical region to investigate why roughly one-quarter to one-third of autistic children remain minimally verbal despite demonstrating strong language comprehension.

    “It gives us a specific place in the brain to look, and a specific question to ask,” Chang noted.

    Equally transformative are the implications for neurotechnology. Today’s speech brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) typically decode intended words from the motor cortex, a strategy that fails if a patient’s motor pathways are severely damaged. Because the lpSTG operates upstream of motor execution, it offers an alternative decoding gateway.

    In proof-of-concept testing with two participants living with severe paralysis and anarthria (inability to speak), the UCSF team successfully decoded both the words participants attempted to say and the words they heard directly from lpSTG signals, pointing toward future conversational BCIs capable of capturing both sides of human dialogue.

    How does this discovery change what we know about how the brain produces speech?

    It has been revealed that for over 100 years, textbooks taught that speech comprehension (Wernicke’s area) and speech production were handled by separate brain systems. UCSF researchers proved that a region inside Wernicke’s area (the lpSTG) actually activates a quarter-second before we speak to build an abstract “blueprint” of each intended word, including its length and syllable count, before sending it to motor areas.

    Why can damage to Wernicke’s area make it hard to speak words, not just understand them?

    Because the neurons that process heard speech sit directly alongside the neurons that build the structural blueprint for spoken words in the left posterior superior temporal gyrus, a stroke or injury to that region disrupts both language comprehension and word planning.

    How could this finding help paralyzed patients communicate?

    Current speech brain-computer interfaces read signals from the brain’s motor cortex, which can be damaged in some paralyzed patients. Because the lpSTG creates word blueprints earlier in the speech pipeline, decoding signals from this region could restore communication for a wider range of paralyzed individuals—and potentially capture both heard and spoken words for natural conversation.

Bowes, Jr. Foundation, and Aligning Research to Impact Autism (ARIA-NSNM-003), which is managed by the Coalition for Aligning Science and funded by the Sergey Brin Family Foundation.

    According to recent reports, disclosures: Alex Silva, Matthew Leonard, and Edward Chang are inventors on a pending UCSF patent application related to this work. Chang is the co-founder of Echo Neurotechnologies, LLC.

    A neural code for generative speech production in human Wernicke’s area.

    Recent findings suggest that wernicke’s area, located in the posterior superior temporal gyrus of the human brain, has long been considered essential for understanding speech. However, damage to this region also disrupts the ability to produce speech, creating a long-standing puzzle in neuroscience. Traditional explanations propose that this area primarily supports speech production indirectly by monitoring sounds during speaking. However, it remains unclear whether this region plays a more direct role in generating speech itself, and if so, what kind of information it represents: sounds, movements, or even properties of whole words. Resolving this question is critical for understanding how the brain constructs language and for developing technologies to restore speech in individuals who have lost it.

    Addressing this question requires probing the human brain at multiple scales with both correlational and causal methods. We combined several complementary approaches, including high-resolution direct recordings of neural populations and single neurons during speaking and listening, electrical stimulation of specific brain regions to test causality, and analysis of patients with localized brain lesions. Across these methods, participants performed a variety of speaking and listening tasks ranging from naturalistic speech to single word repetition, providing a detailed and holistic view of the role of the posterior temporal lobe in generating upcoming speech.

    We identified a specific subregion within individual participants’ Wernicke’s area—the left posterior superior temporal gyrus—that becomes active before speech begins. This early activity precedes word onsets in continuous speech rather than reflecting feedback from hearing one’s own voice. Brain stimulation and lesion analyses showed that disrupting this region causes errors in speech production, confirming its causal role.

    Detailed analyses revealed that this region encodes properties of entire words, such as their length and frequency, rather than individual sounds or motor movements. This is distinct from neighboring brain regions that encode auditory feedback and do so by representing lower-level features such as articulation or sound.

    Recent findings suggest that timing analyses highlighted that activity in this region occurs earlier than in motor areas responsible for controlling speech muscles, placing it at the start of the speech production process. Recordings from individual neurons further confirmed that cells in this region respond before speech production, respond selectively to specific words, and are active during both speaking and listening.

    Finally, in people unable to speak due to paralysis, signals from this region could be used to decode both intended and perceived speech, demonstrating its potential for multimodal brain-computer interface technologies aimed at restoring communication.

    In a recent development, this work identifies a specialized region within Wernicke’s area that generates word-level representations before speech is produced. Rather than serving primarily as a center for speech perception, this region acts as an early stage in the production process, organizing upcoming words before they are translated into motor commands. These findings resolve a long-standing paradox about Wernicke’s area and provide a unified framework for understanding how the brain links language comprehension and production. They also highlight a promising target for future neuroprosthetic devices aimed at restoring speech in individuals with communication impairments.

    #114949. How cognitive behavioral therapy works to treat OCD

    How cognitive behavioral therapy works to treat OCD

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2281 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that clinically reviewed by Dr.
    • Recent findings suggest that obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) can look different from one person to the next.
    • In a recent development, what unites these scenarios is the OCD loop: there’s an unwanted thought or fear, and you do something to make it stop.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

    Recent findings suggest that obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) can look different from one person to the next. For some people, it’s checking the locks again and again, even when they know the door is shut. For others, it’s washing their hands until they feel clean, counting steps or objects, arranging things until they feel just right, or getting stuck on an unwanted thought.

    In a recent development, what unites these scenarios is the OCD loop: there’s an unwanted thought or fear, and you do something to make it stop. But the relief doesn’t last and you end up back at the anxious thought, triggering the process again. For people living with OCD, this cycle can be exhausting.

    Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is one of the most studied ways to break the OCD cycle, and one type in particular, called exposure and response prevention (ERP), has the strongest research support of any talk therapy for OCD. Here’s a look at what CBT for OCD involves, how ERP works, and what a session can feel like.

    In a recent development, CBT is a structured, evidence-based form of talk therapy. It looks at how your thoughts, feelings, and actions feed each other, and it focuses on the present rather than digging through your past. Most versions help you notice unhelpful thoughts and respond to them in new ways.

    CBT for OCD works a little differently. With something like anxiety or low mood, a therapist might help you question a worried thought and look for more balanced evidence. With OCD, that technique can backfire. Trying to argue with an intrusive thought, or prove it wrong, can become a mental compulsion, which keeps the cycle going.

    Sources indicate that so OCD-focused CBT spends less time debating the content of your thoughts and more time changing how you respond to them. The main tool for that is ERP, a type of CBT that focuses on behavior.

    If you've ever been told to "just stop worrying," you may know that advice doesn’t work for OCD. The cycle doesn’t respond to willpower alone.

    Here's how the loop tends to run:.

    You get an intrusive thought or fear you don’t want (the obsession).

    To get relief, you do something to make the feeling go away (the compulsion), like checking, washing, asking for reassurance, or going over events in your mind.

    You feel better, but only for a short while.

    Recent findings suggest that each compulsion can teach your brain that the thought was a true threat and that the ritual kept you safe. So the thought tends to return.

    It has been revealed that say you’re leaving for work. A thought pops up: What if I left the stove on? Your anxiety spikes, so you go back and check. The stove is off, and you feel relief. But on your way to the car, the doubt returns, along with the urge to check again.

    That's why OCD can feel impossible to overcome. The very thing that calms you in the moment is what feeds the cycle.

    Industry observers note that ERP involves gradually facing the things that trigger your fears, while holding off on the compulsion. It can sound intimidating, but it’s planned and step by step, and you and your therapist agree on each move together. Here’s what it tends to look like.

    A lot of questions up front: Early sessions are mostly about getting clear on what's happening. Expect to talk through your intrusive thoughts, the compulsions they trigger, and the situations you avoid.

    Sources indicate that building a fear ladder: Your triggers get ranked from mild to most distressing, and you start near the bottom. You won't be asked to face your worst fear on day one.

    Facing triggers on purpose: You'll meet a fear instead of dodging it, whether that's touching a doorknob, writing down a feared word, or sitting with an uncertain thought.

    Not doing the compulsion: Expect to resist the response you'd normally reach for, even something subtle like seeking reassurance.

    Sources indicate that sitting with the discomfort: At first the fear climbs, which can feel like proof it won't stop. Over time, many people find the fear eases, and they learn they can cope with it.

    Homework between sessions: Practice between sessions is a massive part of progress, so expect to take exposures home and work on them in your daily life.

    ERP with a trained therapist is the core of OCD treatment, and nothing below replaces it. But the stretches between sessions can be long, and a few grounding habits may make them easier to deal with.

    It has been revealed that mindfulness and meditation can help you practice noticing a thought, letting it pass, and not acting on it or trying to prove it wrong. That fits well with ERP, where you also learn to let urges be present without giving in. A few minutes a day can be a gentle place to start.

    Industry observers note that one caution: if you catch yourself meditating to “cancel out” a bad thought, that’s the compulsion sneaking back in. The aim is to let thoughts come and go, not to get rid of them.

    💙 Practice noticing a thought and letting it pass with Chibs Okereke’s short Working With Thoughts meditation.

    When you’re struggling with anxiety or a racing heart, slow breathing can help your body settle. Box breathing is one option, since the even count gives your mind something simple to hold onto.

    In a recent development, use it for everyday stress, like after a tough commute or before bed. During an exposure, or when you’re trying to make a thought go away, it can work against ERP, because the point is to practice facing the discomfort. Ask your therapist when it’s okay to use it alongside your ERP practice.

    💙 For a tense, jittery day, Panic SOS with Kirat Randhawa uses sight, sound, and touch to help your body settle.

    According to recent reports, poor sleep and OCD symptoms often go hand in hand. Research links poor sleep to more intrusive thoughts and harder-to-manage symptoms. Rest may also make it easier to do your ERP practice.

    A steady routine can help. Go to bed and wake up at about the same time each day, and dim the lights and put screens away 30 minutes or so before bed. A warm shower, gentle stretching, or a sleep meditation can help you unwind, and limiting caffeine later in the day may make it easier to fall asleep.

    Recent findings suggest that bedtime can be a hard time for those of us with OCD, as quiet moments can leave room for intrusive thoughts, checking, or reassurance-seeking. If rituals are keeping you up, mention it to your therapist.

    💙 Give your mind permission to power down with this Wind Down (for Sleep) session on Calm.

    In a recent development, putting your obsessions, compulsions, and triggers on paper may help you and your therapist spot patterns you’d otherwise miss. Many people find it easiest to jot down a few quick notes each time the loop reveals up: what set it off, what thought or fear came up, what you did in response, and how you felt afterward. Over time, you may notice that certain places, times of day, or moods make the cycle more likely.

    While you’re mapping the loop, try not to judge yourself or over-analyze your entries.

    💙 If you’re struggling to get started, journaling prompts can help.

    A walk around the block, a stretch, or a few minutes of dancing in your kitchen can help ease stress and give your body a reset. Pick something that feels possible even on a hard day, and tie it to something you already do, like a few minutes of movement while your coffee brews or after you hang up a call. Doing it at about the same time each day can also help it stick.

    One thing to watch for: if movement starts to feel like a ritual, like needing to take a certain number of steps or repeat a routine until it feels “just right,” mention it to your therapist.

    💙 Tamara Levitt’s Mindful Walking series turns a short stroll into a chance to notice what’s around you.

    OCD can be isolating. Talking with a friend or family member you trust can remind you that you’re more than your symptoms. If a loved one wants to help, ask your therapist how. Well-meaning support, like answering the same reassurance question again and again, can accidentally keep the cycle going, and a therapist can guide you both.

    A peer support group can also help. Reputable OCD organizations run groups where you can meet people doing the same work.

    Recent findings suggest that cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is one of the most effective treatments for OCD, especially a type called exposure and response prevention (ERP). Research shows it can reduce symptoms for many people.

    According to recent reports, CBT helps by targeting the anxiety cycle that keeps OCD going. Depending on how severe symptoms are, it's used on its own or alongside medication.

    Sources indicate that exposure and response prevention (ERP) is the best-studied therapy for OCD, but it isn’t the only option. Other approaches include cognitive therapy, acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT), and inference-based CBT (I-CBT). Cognitive therapy helps you examine the beliefs that make intrusive thoughts feel threatening. ACT focuses on making room for uncomfortable thoughts rather than fighting them. I-CBT targets the reasoning that makes an obsession feel believable. Medication, usually a type of antidepressant called an SSRI, is a separate treatment that can lower the intensity of symptoms. It’s often combined with therapy. A clinician can help you weigh which mix fits your situation.

    Recent findings suggest that ERP, or exposure and response prevention, is a type of CBT where you gradually face your triggers while resisting the urge to do a compulsion. It's a first-line treatment for OCD.

    Industry observers note that each time you sit with a fear and resist the ritual, your brain gets evidence that the feared outcome doesn't arrive and that the distress is survivable. That learning is what loosens OCD's grip. A therapist structures the exposures so they stay challenging without tipping into overwhelming.

    Industry observers note that the main difference is what each approach targets. Regular CBT often focuses on changing unhelpful thoughts, such as questioning a worry and replacing it with a more balanced one. CBT for OCD focuses on the compulsion.

    Sources indicate that that’s because, with OCD, the compulsion is what keeps the cycle going. Each time you do the ritual, or try to prove the fear wrong, your brain learns that the thought was a real threat and the ritual kept you safe. In ERP, you face the trigger and hold off on the compulsion. Over time, your brain learns that the feared outcome doesn’t happen and that you can cope with the anxiety without the ritual. Some therapists also work on the beliefs that make intrusive thoughts feel so threatening, but ERP is the main tool.

    Industry observers note that cognitive distortions are unhelpful thinking patterns, and in OCD they often show up as beliefs that make ordinary doubts feel dangerous. Common examples include:.

    Feeling responsible for preventing harm, even when it’s unlikely.

    Overestimating how likely something bad is to happen.

    Thought-action fusion, or believing a thought is as bad as an action.

    Struggling with not knowing for sure (intolerance of uncertainty).

    Assuming a thought must matter because you had it.

    These patterns are common in OCD, and they can fuel the urge to do compulsions. Therapy can help you spot them and loosen their grip.

    💙 Find out more about cognitive distortions and how to reframe negative thoughts.

    Many people see meaningful improvement from ERP within about 12–20 sessions, which is often three to four months with weekly visits (intensive programs can be faster). Some notice shifts with fewer sessions, especially with regular practice in between.

    According to recent reports, timelines vary with symptom severity, how often you practice, and whether medication is part of the plan. OCD treatment is usually designed to be relatively short-term and skills-based, not open-ended.

    You can do some ERP on your own, and self-help books and apps exist for it, but working with a trained therapist is strongly recommended, especially for moderate to severe OCD.

    Self-directed ERP can be tricky to get right. It can be easy to accidentally turn an exposure into a subtle compulsion, or to skip the exposures that matter most. A therapist keeps the blueprint honest and adjusts it as you go. If therapy isn't available right now, guided self-help from a reputable OCD organization is a safer starting point than going it fully alone.

    Mindfulness can support OCD treatment, but it isn't a standalone fix. Research on mindfulness for OCD is promising but mixed, and ERP remains the first-line treatment.

    On its own, mindfulness won't switch off intrusive thoughts, and expecting it to can backfire. Its real value is helping you relate to those thoughts differently, which is why it pairs with therapy rather than replacing it. A clinician can point you toward using it in a way that helps.

    💙 If you’d like to try it, these tips for practicing mindfulness meditation are a gentle place to start.

    #114948. Self-Objectification Alters Brain Response to Media

    Self-Objectification Alters Brain Response to Media

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (899 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A neuroimaging study reveals that women who chronically view their own appearance from an outsider’s perspective, a psychological trait known as self-objectification, exhibit dampened brain activity in aesthetic judgment regions when viewing sexualized images of women.
    • Widespread sexualization of women across advertising, entertainment, and social media has long been linked to societal objectification and broad mental health burdens, including body dissatisfaction, anxiety, and disordered eating.
    • Over time, repeated exposure to objectifying imagery can lead individuals to internalize an observer’s gaze, a psychological phenomenon known as self-objectification, in which a person habitually monitors and evaluates their own body from an outsider’s perspective.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A neuroimaging study reveals that women who chronically view their own appearance from an outsider’s perspective, a psychological trait known as self-objectification, exhibit dampened brain activity in aesthetic judgment regions when viewing sexualized images of women. The findings suggest that internalized beauty standards reshape how the brain regulates and evaluates objectifying media.

    Source: Society for Neuroscience.

    Widespread sexualization of women across advertising, entertainment, and social media has long been linked to societal objectification and broad mental health burdens, including body dissatisfaction, anxiety, and disordered eating.

    Over time, repeated exposure to objectifying imagery can lead individuals to internalize an observer’s gaze, a psychological phenomenon known as self-objectification, in which a person habitually monitors and evaluates their own body from an outsider’s perspective.

    While behavioral studies have established that self-objectification heightens sensitivity to media portrayals, precisely how a woman’s self-perception alters the underlying neural circuitry that evaluates sexualized visuals has remained unclear.

    In a study published today in eNeuro, a research team led by Zhennan Liu at Shanghai Normal University and Haoyue Qian at the Chinese Academy of Sciences investigated how individual differences in self-objectification shape both subjective beauty judgments and brain responses to sexualized imagery.

    Industry observers note that the investigators recruited 60 healthy cisgender heterosexual female participants with an average age of approximately 20 years. First, the team assessed each participant’s baseline level of self-objectification using a validated psychological scale measuring how strongly individuals prioritize external appearance over internal bodily competence.

    Next, participants viewed and rated a series of photographs categorized by the researchers as either:.

    While participants across the board rated the sexualized photographs as more attractive than the non-sexualized images, women with higher self-objectification scores assigned significantly higher attractiveness ratings to the sexualized visuals.

    When the team examined the accompanying brain activity, they uncovered a striking neural signature: women who scored higher on self-objectification exhibited dampened neural activity in brain regions involved in aesthetic judgment while assessing sexualized images.

    Rather than heightened analytical engagement, this reduced activation suggests an altered regulatory or automatic evaluative response when processing culturally idealized, objectifying imagery.

    “Differences between individuals [in this study] may come from how their brains regulate and evaluate the attractiveness of these images,” explained Qian.

    By connecting self-objectification to measurable shifts in aesthetic evaluation circuitry, the study illustrates how internalized social standards leave a functional footprint on visual and emotional processing.

    Looking ahead, the researchers aim to move beyond observational associations to test whether psychological training can buffer the brain against objectifying media.

    “We want to test whether experimentally training or manipulating regulation strategies (e.g., cognitive reappraisal) can change how women respond to and rate sexualized images,” Qian noted. “This will help move the work from association toward causal and intervention-relevant questions.”.

    What is “self-objectification,” and how did researchers measure it?

    Self-objectification is the tendency to view and judge one’s own body primarily from an outside observer’s perspective, prioritizing physical appearance over internal physical capabilities. Researchers measured this trait using a validated psychological questionnaire before participants viewed media images.

    How did self-objectification affect brain responses to sexualized images?

    Women with higher self-objectification scores rated sexualized images of women as significantly more attractive than peers with lower scores, and indicated dampened brain activity in regions responsible for aesthetic judgment, indicating differences in how their brains regulate and evaluate beauty standards.

    Could psychological strategies change how the brain reacts to objectifying media?

    Researchers hope to test whether training cognitive regulation techniques, such as cognitive reappraisal, which helps people consciously reframe how they interpret visual stimuli, can modify brain activity and reduce vulnerability to sexualized media representations.

    Trait Self-Objectification Modulates Attractiveness-Regulating Neural Activity in Sexual Objectification Processing: An ERP Study.

    Contemporary mass media frequently emphasize women’s sexual attractiveness, thereby perpetuating sexual objectification and exacerbating mental distress. Trait self-objectification is presumed to be a risk factor for these adverse outcomes; however, the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying individuals’ responses to sexual objectification remain poorly understood.

    According to recent reports, the present study examined how trait self-objectification modulates behavioral and electrophysiological responses to sexualized female images. Behaviorally, sexualized portrayals of women increased attractiveness ratings, and this enhancement was further modulated by individual levels of trait self-objectification. Neurally, processing sexualized female images evoked a set of ERPs indexing early neurocognitive processes, including perception-related N170 and EPN, and attention-related P200.

    Distinct later neural responses were also identified, including the emotion-related centro-parietal LPP and the regulation-related frontal LPP (f-LPP). Among these sexual objectification-related ERP components, only the f-LPP was modulated by trait self-objectification.

    Furthermore, follow-up analyses revealed that the degree to which trait self-objectification increased individuals’ attractiveness ratings of sexualized images was associated with their reduced f-LPP activity.

    Collectively, these findings suggest that trait self-objectification modulates the processing of sexually objectifying stimuli by altering neurocognitive processes underlying attractiveness regulation, highlighting the importance of this regulatory mechanism in shaping individual responses to sexual objectification.

    The cultural emphasis on women’s sexual attractiveness perpetuates sexual objectification, which is associated with adverse mental health outcomes. Trait self-objectification may modulate these outcomes, yet its relationship with the processing of sexual objectification remains unclear. This study found that trait self-objectification shapes attractiveness ratings during sexual objectification processing.

    Although sexualized images elicited multiple neurocognitive components—N170 and EPN (perception-related), P200 (attention-related), cp-LPP (emotion-related), and f-LPP (regulation-related)—individual differences in trait self-objectification were selectively associated with f-LPP activity. These findings highlight the potential role of attractiveness-related regulatory processing in shaping individual responses to sexual objectification.

    Breaking: The Positive Personality Trait Linked To Having A Crush Outside Your Relationship
